questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Egyptian pharaoh who built the Great Pyramid?
questions.fact: Khufu (also known as Cheops) was the pharaoh who built the Great Pyramid of Giza around 2560 BC. It's the largest of the three pyramids.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Egyptian queen who was the last pharaoh?
questions.fact: Cleopatra VII was the last pharaoh of ancient Egypt. She ruled from 51-30 BC and had relationships with both Julius Caesar and Mark Antony.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient West African empire known for its gold?
questions.fact: The Ghana, Mali, and Songhai empires were all powerful West African empires known for their gold trade. The Mali Empire's Mansa Musa was one of the wealthiest people in history.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the East African trading city?
questions.fact: Kilwa was a major East African trading city on the Swahili Coast. It was a center of trade between Africa, Arabia, India, and China.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Ethiopian kingdom?
questions.fact: Axum was an ancient Ethiopian kingdom that flourished from the 1st to the 8th century AD. It was one of the four great powers of the ancient world.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the slave trade that devastated Africa?
questions.fact: The Atlantic, Trans-Saharan, and Indian Ocean slave trades all devastated Africa. The Atlantic Slave Trade alone transported 12-15 million Africans to the Americas.

questions.prompt: What was the primary characteristic of the name of the European colonization of Africa?
questions.fact: The Scramble for Africa (1881-1914) was the rapid colonization of Africa by European powers. By 1914, almost all of Africa was under European control.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the South African system of racial segregation?
questions.fact: Apartheid was a system of racial segregation in South Africa from 1948 to 1994. It was ended by Nelson Mandela and the African National Congress.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the South African leader who fought against apartheid?
questions.fact: Nelson Mandela (1918-2013) was a South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who became the first black president of South Africa. He spent 27 years in prison.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Ethiopian emperor who modernized the country?
questions.fact: Haile Selassie (1892-1975) was the last emperor of Ethiopia. He modernized the country and was a symbol of African independence.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Algerian War of Independence?
questions.fact: The Algerian War of Independence (1954-1962) was a war between France and Algerian nationalists. Algeria gained independence in 1962.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Kenyan independence leader?
questions.fact: Jomo Kenyatta (c. 1897-1978) was the first president of independent Kenya. He led the country to independence from Britain in 1963.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Ghanaian independence leader?
questions.fact: Kwame Nkrumah (1909-1972) was the first prime minister and president of Ghana. He led Ghana to independence in 1957, making it the first sub-Saharan African country to gain independence.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Rwandan genocide?
questions.fact: The Rwandan Genocide (1994) was a mass slaughter of Tutsi and moderate Hutu by Hutu extremists. An estimated 800,000 to 1 million people were killed in 100 days.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient city in Zimbabwe?
questions.fact: Great Zimbabwe was an ancient city in Zimbabwe that flourished from the 11th to the 15th century. It was the capital of the Kingdom of Zimbabwe.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient trading city in Mali?
questions.fact: Timbuktu was a major trading and learning center in the Mali Empire. It was famous for its universities and libraries and was a center of Islamic scholarship.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Nubian kingdom?
questions.fact: Kush was an ancient Nubian kingdom that existed from around 1070 BC to 350 AD. It was a powerful kingdom that even conquered Egypt for a time.

questions.prompt: What was the primary characteristic of the name of the Zulu kingdom?
questions.fact: The Zulu Kingdom (1816-1897) was a powerful kingdom in southern Africa. It was founded by Shaka Zulu and was known for its military prowess.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Egyptian pharaoh who tried to establish monotheism?
questions.fact: Akhenaten (c. 1353-1336 BC) tried to establish monotheism in ancient Egypt by worshiping only the sun god Aten. His religious reforms were reversed after his death.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the African independence movements?
questions.fact: The African independence movements (1950s-1970s) saw most African countries gain independence from European colonial powers. This period is known as the 'Year of Africa.'

questions.prompt: What year did the American Revolution begin?
questions.fact: The American Revolution began in 1775 with the Battles of Lexington and Concord. The Declaration of Independence was signed in 1776.

questions.prompt: Who was the first President of the United States?
questions.fact: George Washington was the first President of the United States, serving from 1789 to 1797. He's known as the 'Father of His Country' and set many precedents for the office.

questions.prompt: What year did the Civil War begin?
questions.fact: The American Civil War began in 1861 when Confederate forces attacked Fort Sumter. The war lasted until 1865 and resulted in over 600,000 deaths.

questions.prompt: Who was the President during the Civil War?
questions.fact: Abraham Lincoln was President during the Civil War (1861-1865) and issued the Emancipation Proclamation, which declared slaves in Confederate states free.

questions.prompt: What year did the United States enter World War I?
questions.fact: The United States entered World War I in 1917, after years of maintaining neutrality. The sinking of American ships by German U-boats was a major factor.

questions.prompt: What year did the United States enter World War II?
questions.fact: The United States entered World War II in 1941 after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7. The U.S. declared war on Japan the next day.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the economic crisis that began in 1929?
questions.fact: The Great Depression began in 1929 with the stock market crash and lasted until the late 1930s. It was the worst economic downturn in American history.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the program that helped America recover from the Great Depression?
questions.fact: The New Deal was a series of programs and reforms created by President Franklin D. Roosevelt to help the United States recover from the Great Depression.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the movement that fought for civil rights?
questions.fact: The Civil Rights Movement (1950s-1960s) fought to end racial segregation and discrimination against African Americans. It was led by figures like Martin Luther King Jr.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the war fought in Vietnam?
questions.fact: The Vietnam War (1955-1975) was a conflict between North Vietnam (supported by the Soviet Union and China) and South Vietnam (supported by the United States).

questions.prompt: What was the name of the scandal that led to President Nixon's resignation?
questions.fact: Watergate was a political scandal that led to President Richard Nixon's resignation in 1974. It involved a break-in at the Democratic National Committee headquarters and a cover-up.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the first successful English colony in America?
questions.fact: Jamestown, Virginia, was the first successful English colony in America, founded in 1607. It was established by the Virginia Company of London.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ship that brought the Pilgrims to America?
questions.fact: The Mayflower brought the Pilgrims to America in 1620. They established Plymouth Colony in Massachusetts and signed the Mayflower Compact.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the document that declared American independence?
questions.fact: The Declaration of Independence was adopted by the Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, declaring the 13 American colonies independent from British rule.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the war fought between the North and South?
questions.fact: The American Civil War (1861-1865) was fought between the Northern states (Union) and the Southern states (Confederacy) over slavery and states' rights.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the battle that was the turning point of the Civil War?
questions.fact: The Battle of Gettysburg (July 1-3, 1863) was the turning point of the Civil War. It was the bloodiest battle of the war and ended General Lee's invasion of the North.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the amendment that abolished slavery?
questions.fact: The 13th Amendment (1865) abolished slavery in the United States. It was followed by the 14th Amendment (citizenship) and 15th Amendment (voting rights).

questions.prompt: What was the name of the period of rebuilding after the Civil War?
questions.fact: Reconstruction (1865-1877) was the period after the Civil War when the federal government worked to rebuild the South and integrate freed slaves into society.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the movement that gave women the right to vote?
questions.fact: The Women's Suffrage Movement fought for women's right to vote. The 19th Amendment, granting women suffrage, was ratified in 1920.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the attack that brought the U.S. into World War II?
questions.fact: The attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, was a surprise military strike by Japan that brought the United States into World War II.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the program that helped rebuild Europe after World War II?
questions.fact: The Marshall Plan (1948-1952) was an American program that provided economic aid to help rebuild Western Europe after World War II. It was named after Secretary of State George Marshall.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the conflict between the U.S. and Soviet Union?
questions.fact: The Cold War (1947-1991) was a period of geopolitical tension between the United States and the Soviet Union. It was characterized by proxy wars, nuclear arms race, and ideological conflict.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the first man to walk on the Moon?
questions.fact: Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon on July 20, 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission. He said the famous words: 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.'

questions.prompt: What was the name of the fall of the Berlin Wall?
questions.fact: The Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, marking the end of the Cold War and the reunification of Germany. It had divided East and West Berlin for 28 years.

questions.prompt: Which event is considered the starting point of the American Revolution?
options: The Battle of Lexington and Concord
The Signing of the Declaration of Independence
questions.fact: The Battle of Lexington and Concord, fought on April 19, 1775, is considered the starting point of the American Revolution.

questions.prompt: Who was the principal author of the Declaration of Independence?
questions.fact: Thomas Jefferson was the principal author of the Declaration of Independence, which was adopted on July 4, 1776.

questions.prompt: Which treaty ended the American Revolution?
questions.fact: The Treaty of Paris, signed in 1783, ended the American Revolution and recognized American independence from Britain.

questions.prompt: Who was the commander-in-chief of the Continental Army?
questions.fact: George Washington served as the commander-in-chief of the Continental Army throughout the American Revolution.

questions.prompt: Which event involved the dumping of British tea into Boston Harbor as a protest against the Tea Act?
questions.fact: The Boston Tea Party took place on December 16, 1773, when American colonists dumped 342 chests of British tea into Boston Harbor to protest the Tea Act.

questions.prompt: Which battle is considered the turning point of the American Revolution due to the American victory and subsequent French alliance?
questions.fact: The American victory at the Battle of Saratoga in 1777 is considered the turning point of the American Revolution, leading to a formal alliance with France.

questions.prompt: Who was the King of Great Britain during the American Revolution?
questions.fact: King George III was the King of Great Britain during the American Revolution, ruling from 1760 to 1820.

questions.prompt: Which pamphlet, written by Thomas Paine, advocated for American independence and was widely influential?
questions.fact: Thomas Paine's pamphlet 'Common Sense,' published in January 1776, argued for American independence and was widely influential in swaying public opinion.

questions.prompt: Which famous midnight rider warned the colonists of the approaching British forces before the battles of Lexington and Concord?
questions.fact: Paul Revere's famous midnight ride on April 18, 1775, warned the colonists of the approaching British forces, allowing them to prepare for the battles of Lexington and Concord.

questions.prompt: Which American general famously betrayed the Continental Army and defected to the British side?
questions.fact: Benedict Arnold, once a respected general in the Continental Army, famously betrayed the American cause and defected to the British side in 1780.

questions.prompt: Where did George Washington's army spend the harsh winter of 1777-1778, emerging stronger despite the difficult conditions?
questions.fact: George Washington's army endured a harsh winter at Valley Forge in 1777-1778, emerging stronger and more unified despite the difficult conditions.

questions.prompt: What was the purpose of the First Continental Congress, held in 1774?
options: To draft the Declaration of Independence
To petition King George III for redress of grievances
To form a new national government
questions.fact: The First Continental Congress met in 1774 to petition King George III for redress of grievances and to coordinate a response to the Intolerable Acts.

questions.prompt: Which French nobleman played a crucial role in the American Revolution, providing military leadership and securing French support?
questions.fact: The Marquis de Lafayette was a French nobleman who provided crucial military leadership and helped secure French support for the American Revolution.

questions.prompt: Which battle effectively ended the American Revolution, leading to the surrender of British General Cornwallis?
questions.fact: The Battle of Yorktown in 1781 effectively ended the American Revolution, with British General Cornwallis surrendering to the combined American and French forces.

questions.prompt: Which legislative act imposed by Britain on the American colonies required them to provide housing and supplies for British troops?
questions.fact: The Quartering Act, passed in 1765, required American colonies to provide housing and supplies for British troops stationed in the colonies.

questions.prompt: What was the main purpose of the Sons of Liberty, a group formed in the American colonies?
options: To draft the Declaration of Independence
To organize colonial resistance to British policies
To establish a new national government
questions.fact: The Sons of Liberty were formed to organize colonial resistance to British policies, using methods such as protests and boycotts.

questions.prompt: Who famously declared, 'Give me liberty, or give me death!' in a speech urging armed resistance to British rule?
questions.fact: Patrick Henry made his famous declaration, 'Give me liberty, or give me death!' in a speech to the Virginia Convention in 1775, urging armed resistance to British rule.

questions.prompt: Which pamphlet, written by Thomas Paine, argued for American independence and was widely read throughout the colonies?
questions.fact: Thomas Paine's pamphlet 'Common Sense,' published in January 1776, argued for American independence and was widely read throughout the colonies, influencing public opinion.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the document that declared the American colonies' independence from Britain?
questions.fact: The Declaration of Independence was adopted by the Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, declaring the 13 American colonies independent from British rule.

questions.prompt: Which battle was fought on Breed's Hill but is commonly known by another name?
questions.fact: The Battle of Bunker Hill was actually fought primarily on Breed's Hill on June 17, 1775. Despite the name, it was one of the first major battles of the Revolution.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the winter encampment where Washington's army trained with Baron von Steuben?
questions.fact: At Valley Forge, Baron von Steuben, a Prussian military officer, trained the Continental Army in European military tactics, significantly improving their effectiveness.

questions.prompt: What does 'amphibian' mean?
questions.fact: The word 'amphibian' comes from the Greek words meaning 'double life,' because most amphibians live both in water (as larvae) and on land (as adults).

questions.prompt: What are the three main groups of amphibians?
questions.fact: The three main groups of amphibians are frogs and toads (anurans), salamanders and newts (urodeles), and caecilians (limbless amphibians).

questions.prompt: What do frogs start as?
options: The Battle of the Somme (World War I)
questions.fact: Frogs start as eggs that hatch into tadpoles, which live in water and have gills. They then undergo metamorphosis to become adult frogs with lungs.

questions.prompt: What is the largest amphibian in the world?
questions.fact: The Chinese giant salamander is the largest amphibian in the world, reaching lengths of up to 6 feet and weighing up to 140 pounds.

questions.prompt: How do amphibians breathe?
options: With lungs, gills, or through their skin
questions.fact: Amphibians can breathe in different ways: larvae have gills, adults have lungs, and many can also absorb oxygen through their moist skin.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest frog in the world?
questions.fact: Paedophryne amauensis is the smallest frog in the world, measuring only about 0.3 inches (7.7 mm) long. It's found in Papua New Guinea.

questions.prompt: What do amphibians need to survive?
questions.fact: Amphibians need both water and land to survive. They need water for reproduction (laying eggs) and their skin must stay moist to breathe.

questions.prompt: What is the process called when a tadpole becomes a frog?
questions.fact: Metamorphosis is the process by which a tadpole transforms into a frog, developing legs, losing its tail, and developing lungs to replace gills.

questions.prompt: What is the most poisonous amphibian?
questions.fact: Poison dart frogs are among the most poisonous animals in the world. The golden poison dart frog has enough poison to kill 10 adult humans.

questions.prompt: Can amphibians live in saltwater?
options: No, amphibians cannot live in saltwater
questions.fact: Amphibians cannot live in saltwater because their skin is permeable and saltwater would dehydrate them. They need fresh water to survive.

questions.prompt: What is anatomy?
questions.fact: Anatomy is the study of the structure of the body and its parts.

questions.prompt: How many bones are in the adult human body?
questions.fact: The adult human body has 206 bones, though babies are born with about 270 bones that fuse together.

questions.prompt: What is the largest organ in the human body?
questions.fact: The skin is the largest organ, covering about 20 square feet and weighing about 8 pounds.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest muscle in the body?
questions.fact: The jaw muscle (masseter) is the strongest muscle relative to its size, generating the most force per unit area.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest bone in the human body?
questions.fact: The stapes, located in the middle ear, is the smallest bone in the human body, about the size of a grain of rice.

questions.prompt: How many chambers does the heart have?
questions.fact: The human heart has four chambers: two atria (upper) and two ventricles (lower).

questions.prompt: What is the longest bone in the human body?
questions.fact: The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest bone in the human body.

questions.prompt: What is the function of the lungs?
questions.fact: The lungs exchange oxygen from the air with carbon dioxide from the blood.

questions.prompt: What is the brain protected by?
questions.fact: The brain is protected by the skull, a hard bony structure, and cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.prompt: How many teeth does an adult typically have?
questions.fact: Adults typically have 32 teeth: 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars, and 12 molars (including wisdom teeth).

questions.prompt: What is the largest internal organ?
questions.fact: The liver is the largest internal organ, weighing about 3 pounds and performing over 500 functions.

questions.prompt: What connects bones to bones?
questions.fact: Ligaments connect bones to bones, while tendons connect muscles to bones.

questions.prompt: What is the function of the kidneys?
questions.fact: The kidneys filter waste products from the blood and produce urine to remove them from the body.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest unit of life?
questions.fact: The cell is the smallest unit of life, and all living organisms are made of cells.

questions.prompt: What is the function of the stomach?
questions.fact: The stomach breaks down food using acid and enzymes before it moves to the intestines.

questions.prompt: What is the spinal column made of?
questions.fact: The spinal column is made of 33 individual bones called vertebrae that protect the spinal cord.

questions.prompt: What is the function of red blood cells?
questions.fact: Red blood cells contain hemoglobin, which carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body.

questions.prompt: What is the largest artery in the body?
questions.fact: The aorta is the largest artery, carrying oxygenated blood from the heart to the rest of the body.

questions.prompt: What is the function of white blood cells?
questions.fact: White blood cells are part of the immune system and help fight infections and diseases.

questions.prompt: What is the study of body structure called?
questions.fact: Anatomy is the study of the structure of the body, while physiology studies how it functions.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the first emperor of China?
questions.fact: Qin Shi Huang (259-210 BCE) was the first emperor of a unified China, founding the Qin Dynasty and beginning construction of the Great Wall of China.

questions.prompt: What was the purpose of the Great Wall of China?
options: To prevent invasions from the north
questions.fact: The Great Wall of China was built primarily to protect Chinese states and empires from invasions and raids by nomadic groups from the north, particularly the Mongols.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the famous trade route connecting China to the West?
questions.fact: The Silk Road was an ancient network of trade routes connecting China to the Mediterranean, facilitating the exchange of goods, ideas, and culture for over 1,500 years.

questions.prompt: What philosophy was developed by Confucius?
questions.fact: Confucianism, developed by Confucius (551-479 BCE), emphasizes moral values, social harmony, respect for elders, and proper conduct in relationships.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Chinese writing system?
questions.fact: Chinese writing uses characters (汉字), with each character representing a word or concept. There are thousands of characters, making it one of the most complex writing systems.

questions.prompt: Which dynasty is known for its porcelain and the invention of gunpowder?
questions.fact: The Song Dynasty (960-1279 CE) is known for its beautiful porcelain, the invention of gunpowder, movable type printing, and significant advances in science and technology.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Chinese explorer who made seven voyages?
questions.fact: Zheng He (1371-1433) was a Chinese explorer who led seven major voyages during the Ming Dynasty, reaching as far as Africa with a massive fleet.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the longest river in China?
questions.fact: The Yangtze River (Chang Jiang) is the longest river in China and Asia, flowing 3,915 miles from the Tibetan Plateau to the East China Sea.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Chinese civil service examination system?
questions.fact: The Imperial Examination system, established during the Sui Dynasty, selected government officials based on merit through rigorous exams on Confucian classics, creating a merit-based bureaucracy.

questions.prompt: Which dynasty built the Forbidden City?
questions.fact: The Forbidden City in Beijing was built during the Ming Dynasty (1406-1420) and served as the imperial palace for 24 emperors over nearly 500 years.

questions.prompt: Which pharaoh is famous for building the Great Pyramid of Giza?
questions.fact: Khufu (also known as Cheops) built the Great Pyramid of Giza around 2580-2560 BCE, which is the largest of the three pyramids at Giza.

questions.prompt: What was the writing system used in ancient Egypt called?
questions.fact: Hieroglyphics were the formal writing system used in ancient Egypt, consisting of pictorial symbols that represented sounds, words, or concepts.

questions.prompt: Which river was essential to ancient Egyptian civilization?
questions.fact: The Nile River was the lifeblood of ancient Egypt, providing water, fertile soil, and transportation, making agriculture possible in the desert.

questions.prompt: Who was the last active pharaoh of ancient Egypt?
questions.fact: Cleopatra VII was the last active pharaoh of ancient Egypt, ruling from 51-30 BCE before Egypt became a Roman province.

questions.prompt: What was the purpose of the Rosetta Stone?
questions.fact: The Rosetta Stone, discovered in 1799, contained the same text in three scripts (hieroglyphics, Demotic, and Greek), which allowed scholars to finally decode Egyptian hieroglyphics.

questions.prompt: Which ancient Egyptian god was associated with the sun?
questions.fact: Ra (or Re) was the ancient Egyptian sun god, considered one of the most important deities, often depicted with a sun disk on his head.

questions.prompt: What was the process of preserving dead bodies in ancient Egypt called?
questions.fact: Mummification was the elaborate process of preserving dead bodies in ancient Egypt, which could take up to 70 days and involved removing organs and treating the body with natron.

questions.prompt: Which famous tomb was discovered by Howard Carter in 1922?
questions.fact: Howard Carter discovered the nearly intact tomb of Tutankhamun in 1922, one of the most significant archaeological finds in history.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Egyptian capital during the New Kingdom?
questions.fact: Thebes (modern-day Luxor) was the capital of ancient Egypt during the New Kingdom period and was home to the famous Valley of the Kings.

questions.prompt: Which female pharaoh ruled Egypt for about 20 years and is known for her successful reign?
questions.fact: Hatshepsut was one of the most successful pharaohs, ruling for about 20 years and overseeing a period of peace and prosperity, often depicted with a false beard to emphasize her authority.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the city-state that was known for its military society?
questions.fact: Sparta was known for its military society, where boys began military training at age 7 and served in the army until age 60. The city prioritized military strength over arts and culture.

questions.prompt: What form of government was invented in ancient Athens?
questions.fact: Democracy, meaning 'rule by the people,' was developed in ancient Athens around 508 BCE, where male citizens could vote on laws and policies.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the war between Athens and Sparta?
questions.fact: The Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE) was fought between Athens and Sparta and their respective allies, ending with Sparta's victory and the decline of Athenian power.

questions.prompt: Who was the famous philosopher who was sentenced to death by drinking hemlock?
questions.fact: Socrates was sentenced to death in 399 BCE for allegedly corrupting the youth and impiety. He chose to drink hemlock rather than escape, as described in Plato's dialogues.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the temple dedicated to Athena on the Acropolis?
questions.fact: The Parthenon, built between 447-432 BCE, was a temple dedicated to Athena Parthenos on the Acropolis in Athens. It's one of the most famous examples of Greek architecture.

questions.prompt: Who was Alexander the Great's teacher?
questions.fact: Aristotle was Alexander the Great's teacher from age 13 to 16. Aristotle taught him philosophy, politics, and ethics, which influenced Alexander's approach to ruling his empire.

questions.prompt: What were the Olympic Games originally held to honor?
questions.fact: The ancient Olympic Games were held every four years in Olympia to honor Zeus, the king of the gods. The first recorded games were in 776 BCE.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the marketplace and civic center in ancient Greek cities?
questions.fact: The agora was the central marketplace and civic center in ancient Greek cities, where people gathered for commerce, politics, and social activities.

questions.prompt: Who wrote 'The Iliad' and 'The Odyssey'?
questions.fact: Homer is credited with writing 'The Iliad' and 'The Odyssey,' two epic poems that are foundational works of Western literature, though little is known about Homer himself.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the alliance led by Athens?
questions.fact: The Delian League was an alliance of Greek city-states led by Athens, formed in 478 BCE to continue fighting the Persian Empire. It eventually became an Athenian empire.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the first civilization in Mesopotamia?
questions.fact: Sumer was the first civilization in Mesopotamia, emerging around 4500 BC. The Sumerians invented writing (cuneiform), the wheel, and many other innovations.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the first pharaoh of Egypt?
questions.fact: Narmer (also known as Menes) is considered the first pharaoh of unified Egypt around 3100 BC. He united Upper and Lower Egypt.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Greek city-state known for its military?
questions.fact: Sparta was an ancient Greek city-state known for its military prowess. Spartan boys began military training at age 7 and were known for their discipline and bravery.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the first emperor of China?
questions.fact: Qin Shi Huang was the first emperor of a unified China in 221 BC. He built the Great Wall and created the Terracotta Army.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Roman general who crossed the Rubicon?
questions.fact: Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon River in 49 BC, starting a civil war. The phrase 'crossing the Rubicon' means making an irreversible decision.

questions.prompt: What was the primary characteristic of the name of the ancient city destroyed by Mount Vesuvius?
questions.fact: Both Pompeii and Herculaneum were destroyed by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD. The cities were buried in ash and preserved for centuries.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Persian king who invaded Greece?
questions.fact: Xerxes I was the Persian king who led the second invasion of Greece in 480 BC. He is famous for the battles of Thermopylae and Salamis.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Greek philosopher who was sentenced to death?
questions.fact: Socrates was an ancient Greek philosopher who was sentenced to death by drinking hemlock in 399 BC. He was accused of corrupting the youth and impiety.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Egyptian queen who was the last pharaoh?
questions.fact: Cleopatra VII was the last pharaoh of ancient Egypt. She ruled from 51-30 BC and had relationships with both Julius Caesar and Mark Antony.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Roman emperor who built the Colosseum?
questions.fact: Vespasian began construction of the Colosseum in 72 AD. It was completed by his son Titus in 80 AD and could hold up to 80,000 spectators.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Chinese philosopher who founded Confucianism?
questions.fact: Confucius (551-479 BC) was a Chinese philosopher who founded Confucianism. His teachings emphasized ethics, morality, and proper social relationships.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Greek city that was the birthplace of democracy?
questions.fact: Athens is considered the birthplace of democracy. The democratic system developed there in the 5th century BC, though it was limited to male citizens.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Roman general who defeated Hannibal?
questions.fact: Scipio Africanus was the Roman general who defeated Hannibal at the Battle of Zama in 202 BC, ending the Second Punic War.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Carthaginian general who crossed the Alps?
questions.fact: Hannibal Barca was the Carthaginian general who crossed the Alps with elephants during the Second Punic War (218-201 BC). He was one of history's greatest military strategists.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Egyptian pharaoh who built the Great Pyramid?
questions.fact: Khufu (also known as Cheops) was the pharaoh who built the Great Pyramid of Giza around 2560 BC. It's the largest of the three pyramids and one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Greek historian known as the 'Father of History'?
questions.fact: Herodotus (c. 484-425 BC) is known as the 'Father of History.' He wrote 'The Histories,' which chronicled the Greco-Persian Wars.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Roman emperor who converted to Christianity?
questions.fact: Constantine the Great was the first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity. He issued the Edict of Milan in 313 AD, which legalized Christianity in the Roman Empire.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Indian emperor who converted to Buddhism?
questions.fact: Ashoka the Great was an Indian emperor who converted to Buddhism after witnessing the horrors of war. He spread Buddhism throughout Asia and is remembered for his peaceful rule.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Greek mathematician who discovered the Pythagorean theorem?
questions.fact: Pythagoras (c. 570-495 BC) was a Greek mathematician and philosopher. The Pythagorean theorem (a² + b² = c²) is named after him, though it was known earlier.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Roman emperor who 'fiddled while Rome burned'?
questions.fact: Nero was the Roman emperor during the Great Fire of Rome in 64 AD. The story that he 'fiddled while Rome burned' is likely a myth, as the fiddle didn't exist then.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Egyptian pharaoh who tried to establish monotheism?
questions.fact: Akhenaten (c. 1353-1336 BC) tried to establish monotheism in ancient Egypt by worshiping only the sun god Aten. His religious reforms were reversed after his death.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Greek city that was destroyed by Alexander the Great?
questions.fact: Thebes was destroyed by Alexander the Great in 335 BC as punishment for rebelling. He spared only the house of the poet Pindar and the temples.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Roman general who became dictator for life?
questions.fact: Julius Caesar became dictator for life in 44 BC, which led to his assassination by senators who feared he would become a king. His death sparked a civil war.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the ancient Chinese dynasty that built the Great Wall?
questions.fact: The Qin Dynasty (221-206 BC) began building the Great Wall of China, though most of what exists today was built during the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644).

questions.prompt: What does Mesopotamia mean?
questions.fact: Mesopotamia means 'land between rivers' in Greek, referring to the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.

questions.prompt: Which two rivers defined Mesopotamia?
questions.fact: The Tigris and Euphrates rivers defined Mesopotamia, providing water for agriculture and civilization.

questions.prompt: What was the first major city in Mesopotamia?
questions.fact: Uruk, founded around 4000 BCE, was one of the first major cities in Mesopotamia and the world.

questions.prompt: Who created the first known system of writing?
questions.fact: The Sumerians in Mesopotamia created cuneiform, the first known system of writing, around 3200 BCE.

questions.prompt: What was cuneiform?
options: A writing system using wedge-shaped marks
questions.fact: Cuneiform was a writing system using wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay tablets, created by the Sumerians.

questions.prompt: What was the Code of Hammurabi?
options: One of the earliest known legal codes
questions.fact: The Code of Hammurabi, created around 1754 BCE, was one of the earliest known legal codes, with 282 laws.

questions.prompt: Which Mesopotamian empire was known for its hanging gardens?
questions.fact: The Babylonian Empire was known for the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

questions.prompt: What was the ziggurat?
questions.fact: A ziggurat was a massive stepped pyramid temple, the center of Mesopotamian cities and religious life.

questions.prompt: Which king created the first empire in Mesopotamia?
questions.fact: Sargon of Akkad created the first empire in Mesopotamia around 2334 BCE, uniting city-states.

questions.prompt: What was the Epic of Gilgamesh?
options: One of the earliest known works of literature
questions.fact: The Epic of Gilgamesh, written around 2100 BCE, is one of the earliest known works of literature.

questions.prompt: Which Mesopotamian city was known for its library?
questions.fact: Nineveh had a great library created by King Ashurbanipal, containing thousands of cuneiform tablets.

questions.prompt: What was the main economic activity in Mesopotamia?
questions.fact: Agriculture was the main economic activity in Mesopotamia, made possible by irrigation from the rivers.

questions.prompt: What was the wheel used for in ancient Mesopotamia?
questions.fact: The wheel, invented in Mesopotamia around 3500 BCE, was used for transportation and pottery making.

questions.prompt: Which Mesopotamian empire was known for its military prowess?
questions.fact: The Assyrian Empire was known for its military prowess, advanced weapons, and efficient administration.

questions.prompt: What was the role of priests in Mesopotamian society?
questions.fact: Priests in Mesopotamia had multiple roles: religious, administrative, and educational, running temples and schools.

questions.prompt: What was the main building material in Mesopotamia?
questions.fact: Mud brick was the main building material in Mesopotamia, as stone and wood were scarce in the region.

questions.prompt: Which Mesopotamian city was the birthplace of Abraham?
questions.fact: Ur, a major Sumerian city, is traditionally considered the birthplace of Abraham in biblical tradition.

questions.prompt: What was the significance of the number 60 in Mesopotamia?
options: The base of their number system
questions.fact: Mesopotamians used a base-60 number system, which is why we have 60 seconds in a minute and 360 degrees in a circle.

questions.prompt: What was the main god of Babylon?
questions.fact: Marduk was the main god of Babylon, elevated to chief deity when Babylon became the dominant city.

questions.prompt: What ended the Mesopotamian civilizations?
options: Conquest by Persians and later empires
questions.fact: Mesopotamian civilizations ended through conquest, first by the Persians in 539 BCE, then by Alexander the Great and later empires.

questions.prompt: What was the capital of the Roman Empire?
questions.fact: Rome was the capital of the Roman Empire, located in modern-day Italy.

questions.prompt: Who was the first Roman Emperor?
questions.fact: Augustus (originally Octavian) was the first Roman Emperor, ruling from 27 BC to 14 AD.

questions.prompt: What was the Colosseum used for?
questions.fact: The Colosseum was an amphitheater used for gladiator fights, animal hunts, and public spectacles.

questions.prompt: What were gladiators?
questions.fact: Gladiators were fighters, often slaves or prisoners, who fought in arenas for public entertainment.

questions.prompt: What was the Roman Republic?
questions.fact: The Roman Republic was the period before the empire, with elected officials and a senate, lasting from 509 BC to 27 BC.

questions.prompt: What were the Roman legions?
questions.fact: Roman legions were large military units, typically 4,000-6,000 soldiers, that conquered and defended the empire.

questions.prompt: What was the Pax Romana?
options: A period of peace and stability
questions.fact: The Pax Romana (Roman Peace) was a period of relative peace and stability across the empire from 27 BC to 180 AD.

questions.prompt: What was the Forum?
options: The center of Roman public life
questions.fact: The Forum was the center of Roman public life, with government buildings, temples, and markets.

questions.prompt: What were aqueducts?
questions.fact: Aqueducts were engineering structures that carried water from distant sources to Roman cities.

questions.prompt: What were Roman roads?
questions.fact: Roman roads were well-built highways that connected the empire, enabling trade and military movement.

questions.prompt: What was the Senate?
questions.fact: The Senate was a governing body of elder statesmen who advised and made laws in the Roman Republic and Empire.

questions.prompt: What was the fall of Rome?
options: The decline and end of the Western Roman Empire
questions.fact: The fall of Rome refers to the decline and end of the Western Roman Empire in 476 AD.

questions.prompt: What was the Eastern Roman Empire?
questions.fact: The Eastern Roman Empire continued after the fall of the West, becoming the Byzantine Empire, lasting until 1453.

questions.prompt: What were the Twelve Tables?
questions.fact: The Twelve Tables were the earliest written laws of Rome, establishing legal rights and procedures.

questions.prompt: What was a consul?
options: An elected official in the Republic
questions.fact: A consul was one of two elected officials who led the Roman Republic, serving one-year terms.

questions.prompt: What was the study of Ancient Rome called?
questions.fact: Ancient Rome is studied through classical studies, Roman history, archaeology, and Latin literature.

questions.prompt: What was Latin?
questions.fact: Latin was the language of ancient Rome, which evolved into the Romance languages (Spanish, French, Italian, etc.).

questions.prompt: What was a toga?
options: A garment worn by Roman citizens
questions.fact: A toga was a distinctive garment worn by Roman male citizens, a large piece of cloth draped over the body.

questions.prompt: What was the Circus Maximus?
options: A large stadium for chariot races
questions.fact: The Circus Maximus was a large stadium in Rome used for chariot races, holding up to 250,000 spectators.

questions.prompt: What was a triumvirate?
questions.fact: A triumvirate was a ruling group of three men, like the First Triumvirate (Caesar, Pompey, Crassus) and Second Triumvirate (Octavian, Antony, Lepidus).

questions.prompt: What is the largest mammal in the world?
questions.fact: The blue whale is the largest mammal and the largest animal ever known to have existed, reaching lengths of up to 100 feet and weights of up to 200 tons.

questions.prompt: What is a group of lions called?
questions.fact: A group of lions is called a pride, typically consisting of related females, their cubs, and a few adult males.

questions.prompt: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.fact: An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood to the gills, and one pumps blood to the rest of the body. When an octopus swims, the heart that pumps blood to the body stops beating.

questions.prompt: What is the fastest land animal?
questions.fact: The cheetah is the fastest land animal, capable of reaching speeds up to 70 miles per hour (113 km/h) in short bursts covering distances up to 1,500 feet.

questions.prompt: What is a baby kangaroo called?
questions.fact: A baby kangaroo is called a joey. Joeys are born very underdeveloped and continue to develop in their mother's pouch for several months.

questions.prompt: What is the only mammal capable of true flight?
questions.fact: Bats are the only mammals capable of sustained, powered flight. Other mammals like flying squirrels can only glide, not truly fly.

questions.prompt: What is the largest bird in the world?
questions.fact: The ostrich is the largest bird in the world, standing up to 9 feet tall and weighing up to 320 pounds. It's also the fastest two-legged animal.

questions.prompt: How long can a snail sleep?
questions.fact: Snails can sleep for up to 3 years! When conditions are unfavorable (dry or cold), snails enter a state of hibernation or estivation that can last for years.

questions.prompt: What is a group of crows called?
questions.fact: A group of crows is called a murder, one of the most interesting collective nouns for animals. Other groups include a parliament of owls and a pride of lions.

questions.prompt: What percentage of a jellyfish's body is water?
questions.fact: Jellyfish are composed of 95-98% water, which is why they appear almost transparent and can easily be damaged when removed from water.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the famous tower in Paris?
questions.fact: The Eiffel Tower in Paris was built in 1889 for the World's Fair. It's 1,063 feet tall and was initially criticized but has become an iconic symbol of France.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the ancient wonder in Egypt?
questions.fact: The Great Pyramid of Giza is the oldest and largest of the three pyramids at Giza, built around 2580-2560 BCE. It's the only remaining wonder of the ancient world.

questions.prompt: What architectural style is characterized by pointed arches and flying buttresses?
questions.fact: Gothic architecture, developed in the 12th century, is characterized by pointed arches, ribbed vaults, flying buttresses, and large stained glass windows.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the famous leaning tower in Italy?
questions.fact: The Leaning Tower of Pisa began leaning during construction in the 12th century due to unstable foundation soil. It's now a famous tourist attraction.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the famous building in Sydney, Australia?
questions.fact: The Sydney Opera House, designed by Jørn Utzon, is one of the most distinctive buildings in the world, with its sail-like roof structure.

questions.prompt: What is the Colosseum?
questions.fact: The Colosseum in Rome is an ancient amphitheater built in 80 CE, where gladiator contests and public spectacles were held. It could seat up to 50,000 spectators.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the famous bridge in San Francisco?
questions.fact: The Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco is one of the most photographed bridges in the world, spanning 1.7 miles across the Golden Gate strait.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the famous clock tower in London?
questions.fact: Big Ben is the nickname for the Great Bell of the clock at the north end of the Palace of Westminster in London, though it's often used to refer to the clock tower itself.

questions.prompt: What is the Parthenon?
questions.fact: The Parthenon is a temple dedicated to Athena Parthenos on the Acropolis in Athens, Greece. Built between 447-432 BCE, it's a masterpiece of Greek architecture.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the famous building in New York with a pointed top?
questions.fact: The Empire State Building, Chrysler Building, and One World Trade Center are all famous New York skyscrapers with distinctive pointed or spire-like tops.

questions.prompt: Who painted 'Starry Night'?
questions.fact: Vincent van Gogh painted 'The Starry Night' in 1889 while staying at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, France. It's one of the most recognized paintings in the world.

questions.prompt: What art movement is Pablo Picasso most associated with?
questions.fact: Pablo Picasso, along with Georges Braque, co-founded Cubism, an art movement that revolutionized European painting and sculpture in the early 20th century.

questions.prompt: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
questions.fact: Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel between 1508 and 1512, creating one of the most celebrated works of Renaissance art.

questions.prompt: What is the name of Leonardo da Vinci's most famous painting?
questions.fact: The Mona Lisa, painted by Leonardo da Vinci between 1503 and 1519, is perhaps the world's most famous painting and is housed in the Louvre Museum in Paris.

questions.prompt: Which art movement is characterized by visible brush strokes and emphasis on light?
questions.fact: Impressionism, developed in France in the 1860s, is characterized by visible brush strokes, emphasis on light and its changing qualities, and ordinary subject matter.

questions.prompt: Who painted 'The Persistence of Memory'?
questions.fact: Salvador Dalí painted 'The Persistence of Memory' in 1931, featuring melting clocks and becoming one of the most famous surrealist works.

questions.prompt: What is the primary color that cannot be created by mixing other colors?
questions.fact: Primary colors depend on the color model: red, blue, yellow for pigments; red, green, blue for light (RGB); cyan, magenta, yellow for printing (CMYK).

questions.prompt: Who is known for painting water lilies?
questions.fact: Claude Monet painted over 250 works featuring water lilies in his garden at Giverny, creating some of the most famous Impressionist paintings.

questions.prompt: What is the technique of applying paint in thick layers called?
questions.fact: Impasto is a technique where paint is applied in thick layers, creating texture and visible brush or palette knife marks, famously used by artists like Vincent van Gogh.

questions.prompt: Who painted 'Guernica'?
questions.fact: Pablo Picasso painted 'Guernica' in 1937 as a response to the bombing of the Basque town of Guernica during the Spanish Civil War, becoming a powerful anti-war symbol.

questions.prompt: What is artificial intelligence?
options: Machine intelligence that mimics human thinking
questions.fact: Artificial intelligence (AI) is machine intelligence that mimics human thinking, learning, and problem-solving.

questions.prompt: What is machine learning?
questions.fact: Machine learning is a subset of AI where systems learn and improve from experience without being explicitly programmed.

questions.prompt: What is deep learning?
questions.fact: Deep learning is machine learning using artificial neural networks with multiple layers, inspired by the human brain.

questions.prompt: What is a neural network?
options: A computing system inspired by the brain
questions.fact: A neural network is a computing system inspired by biological neural networks, consisting of interconnected nodes (neurons).

questions.prompt: What is natural language processing?
questions.fact: Natural language processing (NLP) is AI that enables computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language.

questions.prompt: What is computer vision?
questions.fact: Computer vision is AI that enables machines to interpret and understand visual information from images and videos.

questions.prompt: What is a chatbot?
options: An AI program that converses with users
questions.fact: A chatbot is an AI program designed to simulate conversation with human users, often used in customer service.

questions.prompt: What is the Turing Test?
questions.fact: The Turing Test, proposed by Alan Turing, tests if a machine can exhibit intelligent behavior indistinguishable from a human.

questions.prompt: What is reinforcement learning?
options: AI learning through trial and error
questions.fact: Reinforcement learning is AI that learns through trial and error, receiving rewards or penalties for actions.

questions.prompt: What is supervised learning?
questions.fact: Supervised learning is machine learning where the AI learns from labeled training data with known correct answers.

questions.prompt: What is unsupervised learning?
questions.fact: Unsupervised learning is machine learning where the AI finds patterns in data without labeled examples.

questions.prompt: What is an algorithm?
options: A set of instructions for solving problems
questions.fact: An algorithm is a set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem or completing a task.

questions.prompt: What is the study of AI called?
questions.fact: The study of AI is called artificial intelligence, a field combining computer science, mathematics, and cognitive science.

questions.prompt: What is a large language model?
options: An AI trained on vast amounts of text
questions.fact: A large language model (LLM) is an AI trained on vast amounts of text data to understand and generate human language.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of AI?
options: To augment human capabilities and solve problems
questions.fact: The purpose of AI is to augment human capabilities, solve complex problems, and automate tasks to improve efficiency.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between AI and machine learning?
options: AI is broader, ML is a subset
questions.fact: AI is the broader field of creating intelligent machines, while machine learning is a subset that enables AI to learn from data.

questions.prompt: What is an expert system?
options: An AI that mimics human expertise
questions.fact: An expert system is an AI that mimics the decision-making ability of a human expert in a specific domain.

questions.prompt: What is the future of AI?
questions.fact: The future of AI includes continued advancement in capabilities, integration into daily life, and addressing ethical concerns.

questions.prompt: What is the impact of AI?
questions.fact: AI is transforming industries, healthcare, transportation, and daily life, while raising important ethical and societal questions.

questions.prompt: What is the origin of AI?
questions.fact: AI as a field began in the 1950s, with the term 'artificial intelligence' coined at a 1956 conference at Dartmouth College.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of China?
questions.fact: Beijing is the capital of China and one of the most populous cities in the world.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Japan?
questions.fact: Tokyo is the capital of Japan and the most populous metropolitan area in the world.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of India?
questions.fact: New Delhi is the capital of India, part of the larger Delhi metropolitan area.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of South Korea?
questions.fact: Seoul is the capital and largest city of South Korea, one of the world's most technologically advanced cities.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Thailand?
questions.fact: Bangkok is the capital of Thailand and one of the most visited cities in the world.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Indonesia?
questions.fact: Jakarta is the capital of Indonesia and the largest city in Southeast Asia.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Vietnam?
questions.fact: Hanoi is the capital of Vietnam and has been a major city for over 1,000 years.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Philippines?
questions.fact: Manila is the capital of the Philippines, though Quezon City is the most populous city.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Malaysia?
questions.fact: Kuala Lumpur is the capital of Malaysia, while Putrajaya is the administrative capital.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Singapore?
questions.fact: Singapore is both a city and a country, serving as its own capital.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Pakistan?
questions.fact: Islamabad is the capital of Pakistan, purpose-built in the 1960s to replace Karachi.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Bangladesh?
questions.fact: Dhaka is the capital of Bangladesh and one of the most densely populated cities in the world.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Myanmar?
questions.fact: Naypyidaw became the capital of Myanmar in 2006, replacing Yangon.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Sri Lanka?
questions.fact: Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte is the capital of Sri Lanka, while Colombo is the commercial center.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Nepal?
questions.fact: Kathmandu is the capital of Nepal, located in a valley in the Himalayas.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Afghanistan?
questions.fact: Kabul is the capital of Afghanistan, one of the highest capitals in the world at 5,876 feet.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Iran?
questions.fact: Tehran is the capital of Iran, located at the foot of the Alborz Mountains.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Iraq?
questions.fact: Baghdad is the capital of Iraq, founded in the 8th century and once the center of the Islamic Golden Age.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Saudi Arabia?
questions.fact: Riyadh is the capital of Saudi Arabia, located in the center of the Arabian Peninsula.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of United Arab Emirates?
questions.fact: Abu Dhabi is the capital of the United Arab Emirates, while Dubai is the most populous city.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the first emperor of China?
questions.fact: Qin Shi Huang was the first emperor of a unified China in 221 BC. He built the Great Wall and created the Terracotta Army.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Chinese dynasty that built the Great Wall?
questions.fact: The Qin Dynasty (221-206 BC) began building the Great Wall of China, though most of what exists today was built during the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644).

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Chinese philosopher who founded Confucianism?
questions.fact: Confucius (551-479 BC) was a Chinese philosopher who founded Confucianism. His teachings emphasized ethics, morality, and proper social relationships.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Mongol leader who conquered much of Asia?
questions.fact: Genghis Khan (c. 1162-1227) founded the Mongol Empire, which became the largest contiguous empire in history, stretching from Eastern Europe to the Sea of Japan.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Japanese period of isolation?
questions.fact: The Edo Period (1603-1868) was a period of isolation in Japan. The country was closed to most foreign trade and contact for over 200 years.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Indian emperor who converted to Buddhism?
questions.fact: Ashoka the Great was an Indian emperor who converted to Buddhism after witnessing the horrors of war. He spread Buddhism throughout Asia.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Chinese dynasty known for its cultural achievements?
questions.fact: The Tang, Song, and Ming dynasties were all known for their cultural achievements. The Tang Dynasty (618-907) is often considered a golden age of Chinese culture.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Japanese samurai code of honor?
questions.fact: Bushido was the code of honor followed by Japanese samurai. It emphasized loyalty, honor, and self-discipline.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Korean dynasty that lasted over 500 years?
questions.fact: The Joseon Dynasty (1392-1897) was the longest-ruling dynasty in Korean history, lasting over 500 years. It was founded by King Taejo.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Chinese explorer who sailed to Africa?
questions.fact: Zheng He (1371-1433) was a Chinese explorer who led seven voyages to Southeast Asia, India, the Middle East, and Africa during the Ming Dynasty.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Japanese period of modernization?
questions.fact: The Meiji Period (1868-1912) was a period of rapid modernization in Japan. The country transformed from an isolated feudal society to a modern industrial power.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Indian independence movement leader?
questions.fact: Mahatma Gandhi (1869-1948) was the leader of the Indian independence movement. He used nonviolent civil disobedience to achieve independence from Britain.

questions.prompt: What was the primary characteristic of the name of the Chinese civil war?
questions.fact: The Chinese Civil War was fought in two phases: 1927-1937 and 1945-1949. The Communist Party, led by Mao Zedong, eventually defeated the Nationalists.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Korean War?
questions.fact: The Korean War (1950-1953) was fought between North Korea (supported by China and the Soviet Union) and South Korea (supported by the United Nations).

questions.prompt: What was the primary characteristic of the name of the Vietnamese War?
questions.fact: The Vietnam War consisted of two phases: the First Indochina War (1945-1954) and the Vietnam War (1955-1975). The latter involved the United States.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Chinese Cultural Revolution?
questions.fact: The Cultural Revolution (1966-1976) was a period of social and political upheaval in China. It was launched by Mao Zedong to preserve communist ideology.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor?
questions.fact: The attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, was a surprise military strike by Japan that brought the United States into World War II.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Indian partition?
questions.fact: The Partition of India in 1947 divided British India into two independent nations: India and Pakistan. It led to massive migration and violence.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Chinese economic reforms?
questions.fact: China's economic reforms began in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping. These reforms transformed China into one of the world's largest economies.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Japanese economic miracle?
questions.fact: Japan's economic miracle (1955-1973) was a period of rapid economic growth. Japan became the world's second-largest economy after the United States.

questions.prompt: What is the closest star to Earth?
questions.fact: The Sun is the closest star to Earth, located about 93 million miles (150 million kilometers) away. It's the center of our solar system.

questions.prompt: How many planets are in our solar system?
questions.fact: There are 8 planets in our solar system: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

questions.prompt: What is the largest planet in our solar system?
questions.fact: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system, with a mass greater than all other planets combined. It's a gas giant with no solid surface.

questions.prompt: What is a group of stars that form a pattern called?
questions.fact: A constellation is a group of stars that form a recognizable pattern in the night sky. There are 88 officially recognized constellations.

questions.prompt: What is the name of our galaxy?
questions.fact: The Milky Way is our home galaxy, a spiral galaxy containing billions of stars, including our Sun. It gets its name from its milky appearance in the night sky.

questions.prompt: What causes the phases of the Moon?
options: The relative positions of the Earth, Moon, and Sun
questions.fact: The phases of the Moon are caused by the changing relative positions of the Earth, Moon, and Sun, which determines how much of the Moon's illuminated side we can see.

questions.prompt: What is a black hole?
options: A region of space with extremely strong gravity
questions.fact: A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape once it crosses the event horizon.

questions.prompt: How long does it take for light from the Sun to reach Earth?
questions.fact: Light from the Sun takes approximately 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel the 93 million miles to Earth, traveling at the speed of light.

questions.prompt: What is a shooting star actually?
questions.fact: A shooting star is actually a meteor—a small piece of rock or dust from space that burns up as it enters Earth's atmosphere, creating a bright streak of light.

questions.prompt: What is the name of Saturn's largest moon?
questions.fact: Titan is Saturn's largest moon and the second-largest moon in our solar system. It has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane and ethane.

questions.prompt: What is astrophysics?
questions.fact: Astrophysics applies physics principles to study celestial objects and the universe.

questions.prompt: What is a black hole?
options: A region where gravity is so strong nothing can escape
questions.fact: A black hole is a region of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.

questions.prompt: What is a neutron star?
questions.fact: A neutron star is the collapsed core of a massive star, incredibly dense with neutrons packed tightly together.

questions.prompt: What is dark matter?
options: Invisible matter that makes up most of the universe
questions.fact: Dark matter is invisible matter that doesn't emit light but makes up about 27% of the universe.

questions.prompt: What is a supernova?
questions.fact: A supernova is the explosive death of a star, one of the most energetic events in the universe.

questions.prompt: What is the speed of light?
questions.fact: The speed of light is approximately 186,000 miles per second (300,000 km/s) in a vacuum.

questions.prompt: What is a quasar?
questions.fact: A quasar is an extremely bright, distant galaxy powered by a supermassive black hole at its center.

questions.prompt: What is the Big Bang?
questions.fact: The Big Bang theory describes the rapid expansion of the universe from an extremely hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago.

questions.prompt: What is a pulsar?
options: A rotating neutron star that emits beams of radiation
questions.fact: A pulsar is a rapidly rotating neutron star that emits beams of radiation, appearing to pulse as it rotates.

questions.prompt: What is dark energy?
questions.fact: Dark energy is a mysterious force that makes up about 68% of the universe and is causing its expansion to accelerate.

questions.prompt: What is a white dwarf?
questions.fact: A white dwarf is the hot, dense core left behind after a star like the Sun exhausts its nuclear fuel.

questions.prompt: What is the event horizon?
options: The boundary of a black hole
questions.fact: The event horizon is the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can escape.

questions.prompt: What is a galaxy?
options: A massive system of stars, gas, and dust
questions.fact: A galaxy is a massive gravitationally bound system containing stars, stellar remnants, gas, dust, and dark matter.

questions.prompt: What is the Milky Way?
questions.fact: The Milky Way is our home galaxy, a spiral galaxy containing billions of stars, including our Sun.

questions.prompt: What is redshift?
questions.fact: Redshift occurs when light from distant objects stretches to longer wavelengths, indicating the universe is expanding.

questions.prompt: What is a nebula?
options: A cloud of gas and dust in space
questions.fact: A nebula is a giant cloud of gas and dust in space, often where stars are born.

questions.prompt: What is the age of the universe?
questions.fact: The universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old, based on observations of the cosmic microwave background.

questions.prompt: What is a singularity?
questions.fact: A singularity is a point of infinite density at the center of a black hole, where physics breaks down.

questions.prompt: What is cosmic microwave background?
options: Remnant radiation from the Big Bang
questions.fact: The cosmic microwave background is remnant radiation from the Big Bang, providing evidence for the universe's origin.

questions.prompt: What is the study of the universe called?
questions.fact: Astrophysics is the branch of astronomy that applies physics to understand the universe and celestial objects.

questions.prompt: Where was the Aztec Empire located?
questions.fact: The Aztec Empire was located in central Mexico, centered around the Valley of Mexico.

questions.prompt: What was the capital of the Aztec Empire?
questions.fact: Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Aztec Empire, built on an island in Lake Texcoco, now Mexico City.

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec name for themselves?
questions.fact: The Aztecs called themselves Mexica, which is why Mexico is named after them.

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec symbol?
options: An eagle on a cactus with a snake
questions.fact: The Aztec symbol was an eagle perched on a cactus with a snake, which appears on the Mexican flag today.

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec religion?
questions.fact: The Aztecs were polytheistic, worshiping many gods including Huitzilopochtli (war god) and Quetzalcoatl (feathered serpent).

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec practice of human sacrifice?
questions.fact: The Aztecs practiced human sacrifice as a religious ritual, believing it was necessary to keep the sun moving and prevent the end of the world.

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec calendar?
questions.fact: The Aztecs used both a 365-day solar calendar and a 260-day ritual calendar, similar to the Mayans.

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec social structure?
options: Hierarchical with emperor, nobles, and commoners
questions.fact: Aztec society was hierarchical with the emperor (tlatoani) at the top, followed by nobles, priests, warriors, merchants, and commoners.

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec agricultural innovation?
questions.fact: The Aztecs created chinampas, artificial islands or floating gardens in lakes, for highly productive agriculture.

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec conquest by Spain?
questions.fact: The Aztec Empire was conquered by Hernán Cortés and Spanish conquistadors in 1521, ending the empire.

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec language?
questions.fact: Nahuatl was the language of the Aztecs and is still spoken by over a million people in Mexico today.

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec tribute system?
questions.fact: The Aztecs required conquered peoples to pay tribute in goods, which supported the empire and capital city.

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec military?
questions.fact: The Aztec military was powerful with elite warrior societies like the Eagle and Jaguar warriors.

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec market system?
questions.fact: The Aztecs had large markets, with the market at Tlatelolco being one of the largest in the world at the time.

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec writing system?
questions.fact: The Aztecs used pictographs and glyphs for writing, though less developed than Mayan hieroglyphs.

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec art?
options: Sophisticated with stone carvings and featherwork
questions.fact: Aztec art was sophisticated, featuring stone carvings, featherwork, goldwork, and codices (books).

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec education?
options: Formal schools for nobles and commoners
questions.fact: The Aztecs had formal schools (calmecac for nobles, telpochcalli for commoners) teaching religion, history, and skills.

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec expansion?
questions.fact: The Aztec Empire expanded rapidly in the 1400s-1500s, controlling much of central Mexico through conquest and alliance.

questions.prompt: What was the Aztec Triple Alliance?
questions.fact: The Aztec Triple Alliance was an alliance of three city-states: Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan.

questions.prompt: What is the modern legacy of the Aztecs?
options: Cultural influence in Mexico and Nahuatl language
questions.fact: The Aztec legacy continues through cultural influence in Mexico, the Nahuatl language, and symbols like the eagle and snake on the Mexican flag.

questions.prompt: What is the main leavening agent in most baking?
questions.fact: Baking powder and baking soda are the main leavening agents in most baked goods, creating bubbles that make dough rise.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between baking powder and baking soda?
options: Baking soda needs acid, baking powder has acid included
Baking soda is for bread only
questions.fact: Baking soda needs an acid to activate, while baking powder contains both an acid and a base, so it activates with liquid and heat.

questions.prompt: What is gluten?
questions.fact: Gluten is a protein found in wheat flour that gives bread its structure and elasticity when kneaded.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of creaming butter and sugar?
questions.fact: Creaming butter and sugar incorporates air into the mixture, creating a light, fluffy texture in baked goods.

questions.prompt: What temperature should butter be for most baking?
questions.fact: Butter should be at room temperature (around 65-70°F) for most baking to properly cream with sugar and mix with other ingredients.

questions.prompt: What is proofing?
questions.fact: Proofing is allowing yeast dough to rise before baking, giving the yeast time to produce carbon dioxide and expand the dough.

questions.prompt: What is a leavening agent?
options: A substance that makes dough rise
questions.fact: A leavening agent is a substance that causes dough or batter to rise by producing gas bubbles, like baking powder, baking soda, or yeast.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of sifting flour?
questions.fact: Sifting flour aerates it, removes lumps, and makes it lighter, resulting in lighter, more uniform baked goods.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between all-purpose and bread flour?
questions.fact: Bread flour has more protein (gluten) than all-purpose flour, making it better for bread that needs structure and chewiness.

questions.prompt: What is blind baking?
options: Baking a pie crust before adding filling
questions.fact: Blind baking is pre-baking a pie crust before adding the filling, preventing a soggy bottom crust.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of eggs in baking?
options: To bind, leaven, and add moisture
questions.fact: Eggs serve multiple purposes in baking: binding ingredients, adding moisture, leavening, and providing structure and color.

questions.prompt: What is the Maillard reaction?
questions.fact: The Maillard reaction is the chemical reaction between amino acids and sugars that creates browning and complex flavors in baked goods.

questions.prompt: What is the ideal oven temperature for most baking?
questions.fact: Most baked goods are baked at 350-375°F (175-190°C), providing even heat for proper rising and browning.

questions.prompt: What is a baker's percentage?
options: A method of calculating ingredient ratios
questions.fact: Baker's percentage is a method where all ingredients are expressed as a percentage of the flour weight, making recipes scalable.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of salt in baking?
options: To enhance flavor and control yeast
questions.fact: Salt enhances flavor, strengthens gluten, and controls yeast activity in bread, making it an essential ingredient.

questions.prompt: What is a sourdough starter?
options: A fermented mixture of flour and water
questions.fact: A sourdough starter is a fermented mixture of flour and water containing wild yeast and bacteria, used to leaven bread naturally.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of chilling cookie dough?
options: To prevent spreading and improve flavor
questions.fact: Chilling cookie dough solidifies the fat, preventing cookies from spreading too much and allowing flavors to develop.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between cake flour and all-purpose flour?
questions.fact: Cake flour has less protein than all-purpose flour, resulting in tender, delicate cakes with a fine crumb.

questions.prompt: What is the study of baking called?
questions.fact: The study of baking is called pastry arts or baking science, combining culinary skills with scientific understanding.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of vanilla extract in baking?
options: To enhance and round out flavors
questions.fact: Vanilla extract enhances and rounds out flavors in baked goods, making other flavors taste more pronounced and balanced.

questions.prompt: What is the windowpane test?
options: A test to check if gluten is developed
questions.fact: The windowpane test stretches a small piece of dough thin enough to see light through it, indicating proper gluten development.
