questions.prompt: How many players are on a baseball team on the field?
questions.fact: A baseball team has 9 players on the field at once: pitcher, catcher, first baseman, second baseman, third baseman, shortstop, and three outfielders.

questions.prompt: How many strikes make an out?
questions.fact: Three strikes make an out in baseball. A strike is called when the batter swings and misses, doesn't swing at a good pitch, or hits a foul ball.

questions.prompt: How many bases are there in baseball?
questions.fact: There are 4 bases in baseball: first, second, third, and home plate, forming a diamond shape.

questions.prompt: What is a home run?
options: Hitting the ball out of the park
questions.fact: A home run occurs when a batter hits the ball out of the playing field, allowing them to round all bases and score.

questions.prompt: What is the distance between bases?
questions.fact: The distance between bases in professional baseball is 90 feet (27.4 meters).

questions.prompt: What is a grand slam?
options: A home run with bases loaded
questions.fact: A grand slam is a home run hit when all three bases are occupied, scoring 4 runs total.

questions.prompt: What is a perfect game?
options: No hits, walks, or errors allowed
questions.fact: A perfect game is when a pitcher allows no batters to reach base - no hits, walks, or errors in 9 innings.

questions.prompt: What is the World Series?
options: Championship between AL and NL winners
questions.fact: The World Series is the championship series between the winners of the American League and National League.

questions.prompt: What is a strikeout?
questions.fact: A strikeout occurs when a batter accumulates three strikes, resulting in an out.

questions.prompt: What is a walk?
options: Four balls, batter goes to first base
questions.fact: A walk (base on balls) occurs when a pitcher throws four balls outside the strike zone, allowing the batter to go to first base.

questions.prompt: What is a double play?
questions.fact: A double play is when the defense gets two outs on a single play, often involving a ground ball to an infielder.

questions.prompt: What is a no-hitter?
options: No hits allowed in a game
questions.fact: A no-hitter is when a pitcher (or pitchers) allows no hits over the course of a complete game.

questions.prompt: What is the distance from pitcher's mound to home plate?
questions.fact: The distance from the pitcher's mound to home plate is 60 feet 6 inches (18.4 meters) in professional baseball.

questions.prompt: What is a save?
questions.fact: A save is credited to a relief pitcher who finishes a game his team wins while preserving a lead.

questions.prompt: What is a bunt?
options: A soft hit to advance runners
questions.fact: A bunt is when a batter lightly taps the ball into play, usually to advance runners or reach first base safely.

questions.prompt: What is a stolen base?
options: Runner advancing to next base during pitch
questions.fact: A stolen base occurs when a runner successfully advances to the next base while the pitcher is delivering the ball.

questions.prompt: What is an RBI?
questions.fact: RBI stands for Run Batted In - a statistic credited to a batter when their hit results in a run scoring.

questions.prompt: What is a curveball?
questions.fact: A curveball is a breaking pitch that curves downward as it approaches the plate, making it difficult to hit.

questions.prompt: What is the All-Star Game?
questions.fact: The All-Star Game is an annual exhibition game featuring the best players from the American and National Leagues.

questions.prompt: What is a shutout?
questions.fact: A shutout occurs when a team prevents the opposing team from scoring any runs in a complete game.

questions.prompt: How many players are on a basketball team on the court at once?
questions.fact: Each team has 5 players on the court at once in basketball.

questions.prompt: What is the height of a basketball hoop?
questions.fact: A regulation basketball hoop is 10 feet (3.05 meters) high.

questions.prompt: How many points is a free throw worth?
questions.fact: A free throw is worth 1 point and is taken from the free throw line after a foul.

questions.prompt: What is the NBA?
questions.fact: The NBA (National Basketball Association) is the premier professional basketball league in North America.

questions.prompt: How long is a regulation NBA game?
questions.fact: An NBA game consists of four 12-minute quarters, totaling 48 minutes of playing time.

questions.prompt: What is a slam dunk?
options: Scoring by putting ball through hoop with hand above rim
questions.fact: A slam dunk is when a player jumps and puts the ball through the hoop with their hand above the rim.

questions.prompt: What is a three-pointer?
options: A shot worth 3 points from beyond the arc
questions.fact: A three-pointer is a shot made from beyond the three-point line, worth 3 points.

questions.prompt: Who is known as 'Air Jordan'?
questions.fact: Michael Jordan earned the nickname 'Air Jordan' for his incredible jumping ability and aerial play.

questions.prompt: What is a rebound?
options: Gaining possession after a missed shot
questions.fact: A rebound occurs when a player gains possession of the ball after a missed field goal or free throw.

questions.prompt: What is a layup?

questions.prompt: What is classical music?

questions.prompt: What is an orchestra?

questions.prompt: What is a conductor?

questions.prompt: What is a composer?

questions.prompt: What is a sonata?

questions.prompt: What is an opera?

questions.prompt: What is a movement?

questions.prompt: What is climate change?
options: Long-term changes in global climate patterns
questions.fact: Climate change refers to long-term changes in global climate patterns, including temperature, precipitation, and weather extremes.

questions.prompt: What is the greenhouse effect?
options: Natural process that warms Earth's surface
questions.fact: The greenhouse effect is a natural process where gases trap heat in Earth's atmosphere, keeping the planet warm enough for life.

questions.prompt: What are greenhouse gases?
options: Gases that trap heat in the atmosphere
questions.fact: Greenhouse gases (like CO2, methane, water vapor) trap heat in the atmosphere, contributing to the greenhouse effect.

questions.prompt: What is the main cause of current climate change?
questions.fact: Current climate change is primarily caused by human activities, especially burning fossil fuels, which increases greenhouse gases.

questions.prompt: What is global warming?
options: Rising average temperature of Earth's surface
questions.fact: Global warming refers to the rising average temperature of Earth's surface, a key aspect of climate change.

questions.prompt: What is carbon dioxide (CO2)?
options: A major greenhouse gas from human activities
questions.fact: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is a major greenhouse gas, with levels increasing significantly due to human activities like burning fossil fuels.

questions.prompt: What are fossil fuels?
options: Coal, oil, and natural gas from ancient organisms
questions.fact: Fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) are formed from ancient organisms and release CO2 when burned, contributing to climate change.

questions.prompt: What is the impact of climate change?
options: Rising sea levels, extreme weather, and ecosystem changes
questions.fact: Climate change impacts include rising sea levels, extreme weather events, ecosystem changes, and effects on human societies.

questions.prompt: What is sea level rise?
options: Rising ocean levels due to melting ice and thermal expansion
questions.fact: Sea level rise occurs due to melting ice sheets and glaciers, plus thermal expansion of warming ocean water.

questions.prompt: What is the Paris Agreement?
questions.fact: The Paris Agreement (2015) is an international agreement to limit global warming to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels.

questions.prompt: What is renewable energy?
options: Energy from sources that don't run out
questions.fact: Renewable energy comes from sources that don't run out, like solar, wind, and hydroelectric power.

questions.prompt: What is the importance of addressing climate change?
options: Critical for future generations and ecosystems
questions.fact: Addressing climate change is critical for protecting future generations, ecosystems, and maintaining a habitable planet.

questions.prompt: What is carbon footprint?
options: Total greenhouse gas emissions from activities
questions.fact: Carbon footprint is the total amount of greenhouse gases (especially CO2) emitted by an individual, organization, or product.

questions.prompt: What is mitigation?
questions.fact: Mitigation means reducing greenhouse gas emissions to limit climate change, through renewable energy, efficiency, and other measures.

questions.prompt: What is adaptation?
questions.fact: Adaptation means adjusting to climate change impacts, like building sea walls, changing crops, and improving infrastructure.

questions.prompt: What is the impact on biodiversity?
questions.fact: Climate change threatens biodiversity through species extinction, habitat loss, and ecosystem disruption.

questions.prompt: What is the role of forests?
questions.fact: Forests absorb CO2 and store carbon, making them important for mitigating climate change.

questions.prompt: What is the importance of individual action?
options: Collective individual actions can make a difference
questions.fact: While systemic change is needed, collective individual actions (reducing energy use, sustainable choices) can contribute to addressing climate change.

questions.prompt: What is the future of climate change?
questions.fact: The future of climate change depends on actions taken now to reduce emissions and adapt to changes.

questions.prompt: What is the study of climate change called?
questions.fact: Climate change is studied through climate science, meteorology, and environmental science, using data and models to understand and predict changes.

questions.prompt: What are clouds made of?
options: Tiny water droplets or ice crystals
questions.fact: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals suspended in the air. When water vapor condenses, it forms these droplets or crystals.

questions.prompt: How are clouds formed?
options: Air cools and water vapor condenses
questions.fact: Clouds form when water evaporates from Earth's surface, rises into the atmosphere, cools, and condenses into tiny water droplets or ice crystals around particles in the air.

questions.prompt: What are the puffy, white clouds called?
questions.fact: Cumulus clouds are the puffy, white clouds that look like cotton balls. They're often associated with fair weather but can develop into storm clouds.

questions.prompt: What are the thin, wispy clouds high in the sky called?
questions.fact: Cirrus clouds are thin, wispy clouds found at high altitudes (above 20,000 feet). They're made of ice crystals and often indicate fair weather or approaching storms.

questions.prompt: What are the flat, gray clouds that cover the sky called?
questions.fact: Stratus clouds are flat, gray clouds that cover the sky like a blanket. They often bring drizzle or light rain and can make the sky look overcast.

questions.prompt: What type of cloud produces thunderstorms?
questions.fact: Cumulonimbus clouds are large, towering clouds that produce thunderstorms, heavy rain, lightning, and sometimes hail or tornadoes.

questions.prompt: At what altitude are clouds typically found?
questions.fact: Clouds are found at various altitudes: low clouds (below 6,500 feet), middle clouds (6,500-20,000 feet), and high clouds (above 20,000 feet).

questions.prompt: What is fog?
options: A cloud that touches the ground
questions.fact: Fog is essentially a cloud that touches the ground. It forms when air near the ground cools and water vapor condenses into tiny water droplets.

questions.prompt: What color are rain clouds?
questions.fact: Rain clouds (nimbus clouds) are typically gray or dark because they're thick with water droplets that block sunlight, making them appear darker.

questions.prompt: How many main types of clouds are there?
questions.fact: There are many types of clouds, but the main cloud types are organized into 10 basic categories based on their altitude and appearance: cirrus, cirrocumulus, cirrostratus, altocumulus, altostratus, nimbostratus, cumulus, cumulonimbus, stratus, and stratocumulus.

questions.prompt: What is the most popular coffee drink in the world?

questions.prompt: Where did coffee originate?

questions.prompt: What is a shot of espresso?

questions.prompt: What is the difference between Arabica and Robusta coffee?

questions.prompt: What is cold brew?

questions.prompt: What is the ideal temperature for brewing coffee?

questions.prompt: What is a macchiato?

questions.prompt: What is instant coffee?

questions.prompt: What is a French press?

questions.prompt: What is espresso crema?

questions.prompt: What is a flat white?

questions.prompt: What is the study of coffee called?

questions.prompt: What is a barista?

questions.prompt: What is the recommended daily caffeine limit?

questions.prompt: What were the two main sides?

questions.prompt: What was the Iron Curtain?

questions.prompt: What are the three primary colors?
questions.fact: Primary colors depend on the color model: red, yellow, blue for pigments (subtractive); red, green, blue for light (additive/RGB); cyan, magenta, yellow for printing (CMYK).

questions.prompt: What color do you get when you mix red and blue?
questions.fact: Mixing red and blue creates purple (or violet). In the subtractive color model (paints), red and blue are primary colors that combine to make secondary colors.

questions.prompt: What color do you get when you mix all the colors of light?
questions.fact: When you mix all colors of light (additive color mixing), you get white light. This is different from mixing paints, where all colors create black or brown.

questions.prompt: What is the complementary color of red?
questions.fact: Green is the complementary color of red. Complementary colors are opposite each other on the color wheel and create strong contrast when placed together.

questions.prompt: What color is associated with stop signs and fire trucks?
questions.fact: Red is associated with stop signs and fire trucks because it's highly visible and attention-grabbing. Red light has the longest wavelength in the visible spectrum.

questions.prompt: What color do you get when you mix yellow and blue?
questions.fact: Mixing yellow and blue creates green. In the subtractive color model, yellow and blue are primary colors that combine to make the secondary color green.

questions.prompt: What is the color of the sky on a clear day?
questions.fact: The sky appears blue because of Rayleigh scattering - shorter blue wavelengths of light are scattered more by air molecules than longer red wavelengths.

questions.prompt: What color is associated with nature and growth?
questions.fact: Green is associated with nature and growth because it's the color of most plants. Chlorophyll, the pigment that makes plants green, is essential for photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: What are warm colors?
questions.fact: Warm colors are red, orange, and yellow - they're associated with warmth, energy, and excitement. Cool colors (blue, green, purple) are associated with calm and tranquility.

questions.prompt: What color is created when you mix red and yellow?
questions.fact: Mixing red and yellow creates orange. In the subtractive color model, red and yellow are primary colors that combine to make the secondary color orange.

questions.prompt: What color do you get when you mix red and yellow?
questions.fact: Mixing red and yellow creates orange. In the subtractive color model (paints), red and yellow are primary colors that combine to make the secondary color orange.

questions.prompt: What color do you get when you mix all colors of paint?
questions.fact: When you mix all colors of paint (subtractive color mixing), you get black or dark brown, not white. This is because paint absorbs light, and all colors together absorb all light.

questions.prompt: What is the complementary color of blue?
questions.fact: Orange is the complementary color of blue. Complementary colors are opposite each other on the color wheel and create strong contrast when placed together.

questions.prompt: What are warm colors?
questions.fact: Warm colors are red, orange, and yellow - they're associated with warmth, energy, and excitement. Cool colors (blue, green, purple) are associated with calm and tranquility.

questions.prompt: What is a shade?
questions.fact: A shade is a color with black added, making it darker. A tint is a color with white added (making it lighter), and a tone is a color with gray added.

questions.prompt: What is the color of the sky on a clear day?
questions.fact: The sky appears blue because of Rayleigh scattering - shorter blue wavelengths of light are scattered more by air molecules than longer red wavelengths.

questions.prompt: What is a primary color?
options: A color that can be made by mixing other colors
A color that cannot be made by mixing other colors
questions.fact: A primary color is a color that cannot be made by mixing other colors. In the subtractive color model (paints), the primary colors are red, yellow, and blue.

questions.prompt: What is a secondary color?
options: A color made by mixing two primary colors
questions.fact: A secondary color is made by mixing two primary colors. In paints, the secondary colors are orange (red + yellow), green (blue + yellow), and purple (red + blue).

questions.prompt: What color is associated with nature and growth?
questions.fact: Green is associated with nature and growth because it's the color of most plants. Chlorophyll, the pigment that makes plants green, is essential for photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: What is the color of the rainbow in order?
options: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet
Red, yellow, blue, green, orange, purple, pink
questions.fact: The colors of the rainbow in order are: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. This is remembered by the acronym ROYGBIV.

questions.prompt: Who composed 'The Four Seasons'?
questions.fact: Antonio Vivaldi composed 'The Four Seasons' (Le quattro stagioni) around 1720, one of the most famous works in classical music, consisting of four violin concertos.

questions.prompt: Who composed 'Für Elise'?
questions.fact: Ludwig van Beethoven composed 'Für Elise' (For Elise) around 1810. It's one of his most popular piano pieces, though the identity of 'Elise' remains a mystery.

questions.prompt: Who wrote the opera 'The Magic Flute'?
questions.fact: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart wrote 'The Magic Flute' (Die Zauberflöte) in 1791, one of his most famous operas, combining comedy, drama, and beautiful music.

questions.prompt: Who composed 'The Well-Tempered Clavier'?
questions.fact: Johann Sebastian Bach composed 'The Well-Tempered Clavier,' a collection of preludes and fugues in all 24 major and minor keys, completed in 1722 and 1742.

questions.prompt: Who composed 'The Nutcracker'?
questions.fact: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky composed 'The Nutcracker' ballet in 1892, which has become one of the most popular ballets, especially during the Christmas season.

questions.prompt: Who composed 'Canon in D'?
questions.fact: Johann Pachelbel composed 'Canon in D' around 1680. Though not well-known during his lifetime, it has become one of the most recognizable pieces of classical music.

questions.prompt: Who composed 'The Ring of the Nibelung'?
questions.fact: Richard Wagner composed 'The Ring of the Nibelung,' a cycle of four epic operas based on Norse mythology, taking over 26 years to complete (1848-1874).

questions.prompt: Who composed 'Clair de Lune'?
questions.fact: Claude Debussy composed 'Clair de Lune' (Moonlight) in 1890, part of his 'Suite Bergamasque.' It's one of the most popular impressionist piano pieces.

questions.prompt: Who composed 'Eine kleine Nachtmusik'?
questions.fact: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart composed 'Eine kleine Nachtmusik' (A Little Night Music) in 1787. It's one of his most famous serenades.

questions.prompt: Who composed 'The Rite of Spring'?
questions.fact: Igor Stravinsky composed 'The Rite of Spring' in 1913. Its premiere caused a riot due to its revolutionary music and choreography, but it's now considered a masterpiece.

questions.prompt: What does CPU stand for?
questions.fact: CPU stands for Central Processing Unit, the primary component of a computer that performs most of the processing inside the computer.

questions.prompt: What does RAM stand for?
questions.fact: RAM stands for Random Access Memory, the computer's short-term memory that stores data temporarily while the computer is running.

questions.prompt: What was the primary characteristic of the name of the first computer?
questions.fact: ENIAC (1946) is often considered the first general-purpose electronic computer, while UNIVAC (1951) was the first commercial computer. Both are significant milestones.

questions.prompt: What does HTML stand for?
questions.fact: HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language, the standard markup language used to create web pages and web applications.

questions.prompt: What does USB stand for?
questions.fact: USB stands for Universal Serial Bus, a standard interface for connecting devices to computers. It was introduced in 1996 and has become ubiquitous.

questions.prompt: What is the name of Apple's operating system?
questions.fact: macOS (formerly Mac OS X) is Apple's operating system for Mac computers. It's known for its user-friendly interface and integration with Apple devices.

questions.prompt: What is a computer virus?
questions.fact: A computer virus is malicious software that can replicate itself and spread to other computers, often causing damage or stealing information.

questions.prompt: What does WWW stand for?
questions.fact: WWW stands for World Wide Web, the system of interconnected documents and resources accessed via the Internet using web browsers.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the first video game?
questions.fact: 'Tennis for Two' (1958) and 'Spacewar!' (1962) are both considered early video games, with 'Tennis for Two' being the first interactive electronic game.

questions.prompt: What does GUI stand for?
questions.fact: GUI stands for Graphical User Interface, which allows users to interact with computers using visual elements like icons, windows, and menus instead of text commands.

questions.prompt: What is conservation?
questions.fact: Conservation is the protection and preservation of natural resources, wildlife, and habitats for future generations. It involves using resources wisely and sustainably.

questions.prompt: What is recycling?
questions.fact: Recycling is the process of turning waste materials into new products. This conserves natural resources, reduces pollution, and saves energy.

questions.prompt: What is the 3 R's of conservation?
questions.fact: The 3 R's of conservation are Reduce (use less), Reuse (use again), and Recycle (turn into something new). This helps protect the environment.

questions.prompt: What is pollution?
questions.fact: Pollution is harmful substances in the environment that can damage ecosystems and harm living things. Examples include air pollution, water pollution, and plastic waste.

questions.prompt: What is an endangered species?
options: A species that is very common
A species at risk of extinction
questions.fact: An endangered species is a species at risk of extinction. Conservation efforts help protect these species and their habitats to prevent them from disappearing.

questions.prompt: What is deforestation?
questions.fact: Deforestation is the cutting down of forests, which destroys habitats, reduces biodiversity, and contributes to climate change. Reforestation (planting trees) helps reverse this.

questions.prompt: What is renewable energy?
questions.fact: Renewable energy is energy from sources that can be replenished naturally, such as solar, wind, hydroelectric, and geothermal energy. It helps reduce pollution and conserve resources.

questions.prompt: What is a carbon footprint?
options: The amount of carbon dioxide you produce
questions.fact: A carbon footprint is the total amount of greenhouse gases (like carbon dioxide) produced by your activities. Reducing your carbon footprint helps fight climate change.

questions.prompt: Why is it important to conserve water?
options: Fresh water is limited and essential for life
questions.fact: It's important to conserve water because fresh water is limited and essential for all life. Only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh water, and much of it is not easily accessible.

questions.prompt: What can individuals do to help conservation?
questions.fact: Individuals can help conservation in many ways: reduce, reuse, recycle; conserve water and energy; use renewable energy; protect wildlife; plant trees; and support conservation organizations.

questions.prompt: How many continents are there?
questions.fact: There are 7 continents: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America. Some models count 6 (combining Europe and Asia as Eurasia) or 5 (combining Americas).

questions.prompt: What is the largest continent?
questions.fact: Asia is the largest continent by land area, covering about 30% of Earth's total land area and containing more than 60% of the world's population.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest continent?
questions.fact: Australia is the smallest continent by land area, though it's also considered the largest island. It's the only continent that is also a country.

questions.prompt: What is the coldest continent?
questions.fact: Antarctica is the coldest continent, with temperatures dropping below -80°C (-112°F). It's also the driest, windiest, and highest continent on average.

questions.prompt: What continent is home to the Amazon Rainforest?
questions.fact: The Amazon Rainforest is located in South America, primarily in Brazil. It's the largest tropical rainforest in the world, covering about 2.1 million square miles.

questions.prompt: What continent is home to the Sahara Desert?
questions.fact: The Sahara Desert is located in Africa, covering approximately 3.6 million square miles across northern Africa. It's the largest hot desert in the world.

questions.prompt: What continent is home to Mount Everest?
questions.fact: Mount Everest, the highest mountain in the world at 29,032 feet, is located in Asia, on the border between Nepal and China (Tibet).

questions.prompt: What continent has no permanent human population?
questions.fact: Antarctica has no permanent human population, though it has temporary research stations. It's the only continent without native human inhabitants.

questions.prompt: What continent is home to the Great Wall of China?
questions.fact: The Great Wall of China is located in Asia, stretching over 13,000 miles across northern China. It was built over many centuries to protect China from invasions.

questions.prompt: What continent is home to the most countries?
questions.fact: Africa has the most countries of any continent, with 54 recognized countries. It's also the second-largest continent by both land area and population.

questions.prompt: What is the most important knife in the kitchen?
questions.fact: A chef's knife is the most versatile and important knife in the kitchen, used for chopping, slicing, and dicing most ingredients.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between sautéing and frying?
options: Sautéing uses less oil and higher heat
questions.fact: Sautéing uses a small amount of oil over high heat with constant movement, while frying uses more oil and can be done at various temperatures.

questions.prompt: What is the Maillard reaction?
questions.fact: The Maillard reaction is the chemical reaction between amino acids and sugars that creates browning and complex flavors when cooking.

questions.prompt: What is mise en place?
options: Preparing and organizing ingredients before cooking
questions.fact: Mise en place (French for 'putting in place') means preparing and organizing all ingredients before you start cooking.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between boiling and simmering?
options: Boiling is vigorous, simmering is gentle
questions.fact: Boiling is when liquid reaches 212°F with large bubbles, while simmering is a gentle boil around 180-200°F with small bubbles.

questions.prompt: What is braising?
options: Cooking with moist heat in a covered pot
questions.fact: Braising is a cooking method that combines searing and then slow cooking with moist heat in a covered pot, perfect for tough cuts of meat.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of resting meat after cooking?
questions.fact: Resting meat allows juices to redistribute throughout the meat, resulting in more tender and flavorful results.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between herbs and spices?
options: Herbs are leaves, spices are seeds/barks/roots
questions.fact: Herbs are the leaves of plants (like basil, thyme), while spices come from other parts like seeds, bark, roots, or fruits (like cinnamon, pepper).

questions.prompt: What is deglazing?
options: Adding liquid to a hot pan to release browned bits
questions.fact: Deglazing is adding liquid (wine, stock, etc.) to a hot pan to release browned bits stuck to the bottom, creating a flavorful sauce.

questions.prompt: What is the danger zone for food?
questions.fact: The danger zone is 40-140°F (4-60°C), where bacteria multiply rapidly. Food should not be left in this range for more than 2 hours.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of salt in cooking?
options: To enhance flavor and preserve food
questions.fact: Salt enhances flavors, helps preserve food, and can draw out moisture or help retain it depending on how it's used.

questions.prompt: What is a roux?
options: A mixture of flour and fat used to thicken
questions.fact: A roux is a mixture of equal parts flour and fat (usually butter) cooked together, used to thicken sauces and soups.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between stock and broth?
options: Stock is made with bones, broth is made with meat
questions.fact: Stock is made by simmering bones (often with vegetables), while broth is made by simmering meat. Stock is typically richer and more gelatinous.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of marinating?
questions.fact: Marinating adds flavor and can help tenderize meat by breaking down proteins, especially with acidic ingredients like vinegar or citrus.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between dicing and mincing?
options: Dicing is larger cubes, mincing is very fine
questions.fact: Dicing creates uniform cubes (small, medium, or large), while mincing is cutting into very fine pieces, often for garlic or herbs.

questions.prompt: What is the study of cooking called?
questions.fact: The study of cooking involves culinary arts (technique and creativity) and food science (the chemistry and physics of cooking).

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of acid in cooking?
options: To brighten flavors and balance richness
questions.fact: Acid (lemon juice, vinegar) brightens flavors, balances richness, and can help tenderize proteins.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between baking and roasting?
options: Baking is for bread/cakes, roasting is for meats/vegetables
questions.fact: Baking typically refers to cooking bread, cakes, and pastries, while roasting refers to cooking meats and vegetables in dry heat.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a food thermometer?
options: To ensure food is cooked to safe temperature
questions.fact: A food thermometer ensures food reaches safe internal temperatures, preventing foodborne illness (165°F for poultry, 145°F for beef, etc.).

questions.prompt: What is the difference between searing and grilling?
options: Searing is in a pan, grilling is over direct heat
questions.fact: Searing is cooking at high heat in a pan to create a browned crust, while grilling is cooking over direct heat (gas, charcoal, or electric).

questions.prompt: What is the largest country in the world by land area?
questions.fact: Russia is the largest country in the world by land area, covering about 6.6 million square miles (17.1 million square kilometers), spanning 11 time zones.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest country in the world?
questions.fact: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world, covering only 0.17 square miles (0.44 square kilometers) and located entirely within Rome, Italy.

questions.prompt: Which country has the most people?
questions.fact: China has the largest population in the world, with over 1.4 billion people, though India is close behind and may soon surpass it.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Canada?
questions.fact: Ottawa is the capital of Canada, chosen as a compromise between English-speaking Toronto and French-speaking Montreal. It's located in the province of Ontario.

questions.prompt: Which country is known as the 'Land of the Rising Sun'?
questions.fact: Japan is known as the 'Land of the Rising Sun' because the Japanese name for Japan, 'Nihon' or 'Nippon,' means 'origin of the sun' or 'sun's origin.'

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Australia?
questions.fact: Canberra is the capital of Australia, a planned city built specifically to serve as the capital. Sydney and Melbourne are larger cities but Canberra was chosen as a compromise.

questions.prompt: Which country is home to the Eiffel Tower?
questions.fact: The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris, France. It was built in 1889 for the World's Fair and was initially criticized but has become an iconic symbol of France.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Brazil?
questions.fact: Brasília is the capital of Brazil, a planned city built in the 1960s. It's known for its modernist architecture and was designed to be the country's capital.

questions.prompt: Which country is known for the Great Wall?
questions.fact: The Great Wall of China is one of the most famous landmarks in the world, stretching over 13,000 miles and built over many centuries to protect China from invasions.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Egypt?
questions.fact: Cairo is the capital and largest city of Egypt, located on the banks of the Nile River. It's one of the largest cities in Africa and the Middle East.

questions.prompt: What is country music?
options: Music with rural themes and storytelling
questions.fact: Country music features rural themes, storytelling, and often includes instruments like guitar, fiddle, and banjo.

questions.prompt: What is the origin of country music?
questions.fact: Country music originated in the American South and Appalachia, blending folk, blues, and gospel traditions.

questions.prompt: What instrument is central to country music?
questions.fact: The guitar is central to country music, often acoustic in traditional country and electric in modern country.

questions.prompt: What is a fiddle?
options: A violin played in country style
questions.fact: A fiddle is a violin played in country or folk style, with a distinctive playing technique.

questions.prompt: What is a banjo?
options: A string instrument with a round body
questions.fact: A banjo is a string instrument with a round body and distinctive twangy sound, common in country and bluegrass.

questions.prompt: What is bluegrass?
questions.fact: Bluegrass is a subgenre of country music with fast tempos, acoustic instruments, and tight harmonies.

questions.prompt: What is Nashville?
questions.fact: Nashville, Tennessee is known as 'Music City' and is the capital of country music.

questions.prompt: What is the Grand Ole Opry?
questions.fact: The Grand Ole Opry is a famous country music venue and radio show in Nashville, running since 1925.

questions.prompt: What is a country ballad?
questions.fact: A country ballad is a slow, emotional song that tells a story, often about love or heartbreak.

questions.prompt: What is honky-tonk?
options: A style of country music and a type of bar
questions.fact: Honky-tonk is both a style of country music with a danceable beat and a type of bar where it's played.

questions.prompt: What is a country star?
questions.fact: A country star is a famous, successful country musician with a large following.

questions.prompt: What is the study of country music called?
questions.fact: Country music is studied through musicology, cultural studies, and country music history.

questions.prompt: What is a country album?
questions.fact: A country album is a collection of country songs released together, typically on CD, vinyl, or digital format.

questions.prompt: What is a steel guitar?
options: A guitar with a distinctive sliding sound
questions.fact: A steel guitar is played with a steel bar, creating a distinctive sliding, twangy sound common in country music.

questions.prompt: What is a country concert?
options: A live performance of country music
questions.fact: A country concert is a live performance where country artists play for an audience.

questions.prompt: What is a country song typically about?
questions.fact: Country songs typically tell stories about love, heartbreak, rural life, family, and working-class experiences.

questions.prompt: What is a country band?
questions.fact: A country band is a group of musicians who play country music together, typically with guitar, bass, drums, and other instruments.

questions.prompt: What is a country music festival?
options: A multi-day event featuring country music
questions.fact: A country music festival is a multi-day event featuring multiple country performances and artists.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the country music awards?
questions.fact: The CMAs (Country Music Association Awards) are the premier awards for country music.

questions.prompt: What is a country legend?
questions.fact: A country legend is a highly influential country musician who has made significant contributions to the genre.

questions.prompt: How many players are on a cricket team?
questions.fact: Each cricket team has 11 players on the field at once.

questions.prompt: What is a wicket?
questions.fact: A wicket consists of three stumps with two bails on top, which the bowler tries to hit.

questions.prompt: What is a run?
questions.fact: A run is scored when batsmen run between the wickets after the ball is hit.

questions.prompt: What is a batsman?
options: A player who hits the ball
questions.fact: A batsman (or batter) is the player who tries to hit the ball and score runs.

questions.prompt: What is a bowler?
options: A player who throws the ball
questions.fact: A bowler is the player who throws (bowls) the ball toward the batsman.

questions.prompt: What is an over?
questions.fact: An over consists of six legal deliveries (balls) bowled by the same bowler.

questions.prompt: What is a century?
questions.fact: A century is when a batsman scores 100 runs in a single innings.

questions.prompt: What is a six?
options: Hitting ball over boundary without bouncing
questions.fact: A six is scored when the batsman hits the ball over the boundary without it bouncing, worth 6 runs.

questions.prompt: What is a four?
questions.fact: A four is scored when the ball reaches the boundary after bouncing, worth 4 runs.

questions.prompt: What is an innings?
questions.fact: An innings is a team's turn to bat, which continues until 10 wickets fall or overs are completed.

questions.prompt: What is a test match?
questions.fact: A test match is the longest form of cricket, played over five days with unlimited overs.

questions.prompt: What is a one-day match?
questions.fact: A one-day match (ODI) is limited to 50 overs per team, completed in one day.

questions.prompt: What is a T20?
questions.fact: T20 is the shortest form of cricket, with each team batting for 20 overs, typically lasting 3 hours.

questions.prompt: What is LBW?
questions.fact: LBW (Leg Before Wicket) is a way to dismiss a batsman if the ball hits their leg in front of the wicket.

questions.prompt: What is a catch?
options: Catching the ball to dismiss batsman
questions.fact: A catch occurs when a fielder catches the ball hit by the batsman before it bounces, dismissing the batsman.

questions.prompt: What is a stumping?
questions.fact: A stumping occurs when the wicket-keeper removes the bails while the batsman is out of their crease.

questions.prompt: What is the study of cricket called?
questions.fact: Cricket is simply called cricket, though it's studied and analyzed by coaches and statisticians.

questions.prompt: What is a boundary?
questions.fact: The boundary is the edge of the playing field, and hitting the ball over it scores 4 or 6 runs.

questions.prompt: What is the Ashes?
options: A test series between England and Australia
questions.fact: The Ashes is a prestigious test cricket series played between England and Australia.

questions.prompt: What is cryptocurrency?
questions.fact: Cryptocurrency is digital currency that uses cryptography for security and operates independently of central banks.

questions.prompt: What is Bitcoin?
options: The first and most famous cryptocurrency
questions.fact: Bitcoin, created in 2009, was the first cryptocurrency and remains the most valuable and well-known.

questions.prompt: What is blockchain?
questions.fact: Blockchain is a distributed ledger technology that records transactions across many computers, making it secure and transparent.

questions.prompt: What is mining?
options: The process of validating transactions and creating new coins
questions.fact: Mining is the process of validating cryptocurrency transactions and creating new coins by solving complex mathematical problems.

questions.prompt: What is a wallet?
questions.fact: A cryptocurrency wallet is software or hardware that stores the keys needed to access and manage your cryptocurrency.

questions.prompt: What is the study of cryptocurrency called?
questions.fact: Cryptocurrency is studied through blockchain technology, cryptography, and digital finance research.

questions.prompt: What is the impact of cryptocurrency?
questions.fact: Cryptocurrency is transforming finance, enabling decentralized transactions and new forms of digital money.

questions.prompt: What is the origin of cryptocurrency?
questions.fact: Cryptocurrency began with Bitcoin in 2009, created by an anonymous person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto.

questions.prompt: What is the future of cryptocurrency?
questions.fact: The future of cryptocurrency includes wider adoption, new use cases, and integration with traditional finance.

questions.prompt: What is the importance of cryptocurrency?
options: Potential to transform finance and transactions
questions.fact: Cryptocurrency has the potential to transform finance, enable decentralized transactions, and create new economic systems.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between cryptocurrency and traditional currency?
questions.fact: Cryptocurrency is decentralized (no central authority) and purely digital, while traditional currency is centralized and can be physical.

questions.prompt: What is the impact of cryptocurrency on finance?
options: Challenging traditional banking and payment systems
questions.fact: Cryptocurrency is challenging traditional banking and payment systems, enabling peer-to-peer transactions without intermediaries.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies?
options: Bitcoin was first, others are alternatives
questions.fact: Bitcoin was the first cryptocurrency, while others (altcoins) are alternatives with different features and purposes.

questions.prompt: What is the impact of cryptocurrency on society?
options: Potential to change how people transact and store value
questions.fact: Cryptocurrency has the potential to change how people transact, store value, and interact with financial systems.

questions.prompt: What is the currency of the United States?

questions.prompt: What is the currency of the United Kingdom?

questions.prompt: What is the currency of Japan?

questions.prompt: What is the currency used by most European Union countries?

questions.prompt: What is the currency of China?

questions.prompt: What is cybersecurity?
questions.fact: Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting computer systems, networks, and data from digital attacks and unauthorized access.

questions.prompt: What is a virus?
questions.fact: A computer virus is malicious software that replicates itself and spreads to other computers, often causing damage.

questions.prompt: What is malware?
questions.fact: Malware (malicious software) is any software designed to harm or exploit computer systems, including viruses, trojans, and ransomware.

questions.prompt: What is a firewall?
questions.fact: A firewall is a security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on security rules.

questions.prompt: What is encryption?
questions.fact: Encryption is the process of scrambling data so only authorized parties can read it, protecting information from unauthorized access.

questions.prompt: What is a password?
questions.fact: A password is a secret code used to authenticate and verify a user's identity when accessing systems or accounts.

questions.prompt: What is phishing?
questions.fact: Phishing is fraudulent attempts to steal sensitive information by pretending to be a trustworthy entity, often via email.

questions.prompt: What is two-factor authentication?
questions.fact: Two-factor authentication (2FA) requires two methods to verify identity, like a password plus a code from your phone.

questions.prompt: What is a hacker?
questions.fact: A hacker is someone who accesses computer systems, which can be ethical (white hat) or malicious (black hat).

questions.prompt: What is ransomware?
options: Malware that locks data until payment
questions.fact: Ransomware is malware that encrypts a victim's data and demands payment (ransom) to restore access.

questions.prompt: What is the study of cybersecurity called?
questions.fact: Cybersecurity is also called information security or computer security, involving protecting digital information and systems.

questions.prompt: What is a data breach?
questions.fact: A data breach is an incident where sensitive, protected, or confidential data is accessed or disclosed without authorization.

questions.prompt: What is the importance of cybersecurity?
questions.fact: Cybersecurity is crucial for protecting personal information, financial data, and critical infrastructure from cyber threats.

questions.prompt: What is a VPN?
options: A virtual private network for secure connection
questions.fact: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) creates a secure, encrypted connection over the internet, protecting your online activity.

questions.prompt: What is the impact of cyber attacks?
options: Data loss, financial damage, and privacy violations
questions.fact: Cyber attacks can cause data loss, financial damage, privacy violations, and disruption of services.

questions.prompt: What is the future of cybersecurity?
questions.fact: The future of cybersecurity involves evolving threats (AI-powered attacks) and new defenses (AI-powered security).

questions.prompt: What is the origin of cybersecurity?
questions.fact: Cybersecurity emerged in the 1970s-1980s as computers became networked and security threats increased.

questions.prompt: What is a security patch?
options: A software update that fixes vulnerabilities
questions.fact: A security patch is a software update that fixes vulnerabilities and security flaws in programs or systems.

questions.prompt: What is the importance of strong passwords?
questions.fact: Strong passwords are essential for protecting accounts from unauthorized access and should be unique and complex.

questions.prompt: What is the Tour de France?
questions.fact: The Tour de France is the most prestigious multi-stage cycling race, covering over 2,000 miles in about 3 weeks.

questions.prompt: What is a peloton?
questions.fact: The peloton is the main group of riders in a race, where cyclists draft behind each other to save energy.

questions.prompt: What is drafting?
options: Riding behind another cyclist to reduce wind resistance
questions.fact: Drafting is riding closely behind another cyclist to reduce wind resistance and save energy.

questions.prompt: What is a breakaway?
options: Riders who escape from the peloton
questions.fact: A breakaway is when one or more riders escape from the main peloton to try to win the race.

questions.prompt: What is a time trial?
options: Riders start individually against the clock
questions.fact: A time trial is a race where riders start individually and race against the clock, not other riders.

questions.prompt: What is a sprint?
questions.fact: A sprint is a fast finish where riders compete for position at the end of a race or stage.

questions.prompt: What is a stage?
questions.fact: A stage is a single day of racing in a multi-day race like the Tour de France.

questions.prompt: What is the yellow jersey?
questions.fact: The yellow jersey (maillot jaune) is worn by the overall race leader in the Tour de France.

questions.prompt: What is a mountain stage?
questions.fact: A mountain stage features significant climbs and is often where the race is won or lost.

questions.prompt: What is a domestique?
questions.fact: A domestique is a support rider who helps the team leader by fetching water, blocking wind, and sacrificing their own chances.

questions.prompt: What is a chain?
options: The metal links that drive the bike
questions.fact: The chain transfers power from the pedals to the rear wheel, driving the bicycle forward.

questions.prompt: What is a derailleur?
options: A mechanism that moves the chain between gears
questions.fact: A derailleur is the mechanism that moves the chain between different gears on a bicycle.

questions.prompt: What is a criterium?
options: A short race on a closed circuit
questions.fact: A criterium is a short, fast race on a closed circuit, typically less than 3 miles per lap.

questions.prompt: What is a fixie?
questions.fact: A fixie (fixed-gear) is a bicycle with no freewheel, so the pedals always move when the bike is moving.

questions.prompt: What is a wheelie?
options: Riding on the rear wheel only
questions.fact: A wheelie is a trick where the rider lifts the front wheel and rides on only the rear wheel.

questions.prompt: What is the study of cycling called?
questions.fact: Cycling is simply called cycling, though it's studied and analyzed by coaches and sports scientists.

questions.prompt: What is a time trial bike?
options: An aerodynamic bike for time trials
questions.fact: A time trial bike is designed for aerodynamics, with features to reduce wind resistance.

questions.prompt: What is a grand tour?
questions.fact: A grand tour is a three-week stage race, including the Tour de France, Giro d'Italia, and Vuelta a España.

questions.prompt: What is a puncture?
questions.fact: A puncture is when a tire is damaged and loses air, commonly called a flat tire.

questions.prompt: What is the largest desert in the world?
questions.fact: The Antarctic Desert is the largest desert in the world, covering about 5.5 million square miles, though it's covered in ice.

questions.prompt: What is the largest hot desert in the world?
questions.fact: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world, covering about 3.6 million square miles across North Africa.

questions.prompt: What is a desert?
questions.fact: A desert is an area that receives very little precipitation, less than 10 inches per year, and can be hot or cold.

questions.prompt: What is the study of deserts called?
questions.fact: Deserts are studied through geography, ecology, and arid land studies, exploring their unique ecosystems.

questions.prompt: What is the importance of deserts?
questions.fact: Deserts have unique ecosystems, support specialized plants and animals, and can contain valuable mineral resources.

questions.prompt: What is the impact of deserts?
questions.fact: Deserts are important ecosystems, influence climate, and are home to unique plants and animals adapted to arid conditions.

questions.prompt: What does the word 'dinosaur' mean?
questions.fact: The word 'dinosaur' comes from the Greek words 'deinos' (terrible) and 'sauros' (lizard), meaning 'terrible lizard,' coined by Sir Richard Owen in 1842.

questions.prompt: What is the largest known dinosaur?
questions.fact: Argentinosaurus is considered the largest known dinosaur, estimated to have been 100-130 feet long and weighing 80-100 tons, though new discoveries continue to challenge this.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the most famous dinosaur?
questions.fact: Tyrannosaurus Rex, often called T. rex, is the most famous dinosaur, known for its massive size, powerful jaws, and tiny arms. It lived about 68-66 million years ago.

questions.prompt: When did dinosaurs go extinct?
questions.fact: Dinosaurs (except birds) went extinct approximately 65 million years ago, likely due to an asteroid impact that caused massive climate change.

questions.prompt: What are birds considered to be?
questions.fact: Birds are considered living dinosaurs, descended from theropod dinosaurs. Modern birds are the only surviving lineage of dinosaurs.

questions.prompt: What period did the T. rex live in?
questions.fact: Tyrannosaurus Rex lived during the Late Cretaceous period, about 68-66 million years ago, making it one of the last non-avian dinosaurs.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the dinosaur with three horns on its head?
questions.fact: Triceratops was a large herbivorous dinosaur with three horns on its head - two large ones above the eyes and a smaller one on the nose - and a bony frill.

questions.prompt: What was the smallest known dinosaur?
questions.fact: The smallest dinosaurs were about the size of chickens. Compsognathus, Microraptor, and Archaeopteryx are all candidates for the smallest, each about 1-2 feet long.

questions.prompt: What is the name for the study of dinosaurs?
questions.fact: Paleontology is the study of ancient life, including dinosaurs. Paleontologists study fossils to understand how dinosaurs lived, evolved, and went extinct.

questions.prompt: What dinosaur had plates on its back?
questions.fact: Stegosaurus had distinctive plates along its back and spikes on its tail. The purpose of the plates is still debated - they may have been for temperature regulation or display.

questions.prompt: What was the first Disney animated feature film?
options: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
questions.fact: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, released in 1937, was the first full-length animated feature film and the first Disney animated feature. It revolutionized animation.

questions.prompt: What animation technique did Disney pioneer for Snow White?
questions.fact: Disney pioneered the multiplane camera for Snow White, which created depth and dimension in animated films by using multiple layers of artwork.

questions.prompt: What was the first Disney film to use xerography (photocopying) for animation?
questions.fact: 101 Dalmatians, released in 1961, was the first Disney film to use xerography, which allowed animators to photocopy drawings directly onto animation cels, saving time and money.

questions.prompt: What was the first Disney film to use computer-generated imagery (CGI)?
questions.fact: The Great Mouse Detective, released in 1986, was the first Disney film to use computer-generated imagery for the clock tower sequence, marking the beginning of Disney's use of CGI.

questions.prompt: What was the first Disney film to be entirely computer-animated?

questions.prompt: What animation technique did Disney use for the ballroom scene in Beauty and the Beast?

questions.prompt: What was the name of the animation software developed by Disney for The Little Mermaid?

questions.prompt: What was the first Disney film to use the multiplane camera?
options: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
questions.fact: Pinocchio, released in 1940, was the first Disney film to fully utilize the multiplane camera, creating stunning depth and dimension in the animation.

questions.prompt: What animation technique did Disney use for the water effects in Moana?
questions.fact: Moana used advanced computer-generated imagery for the water effects, creating realistic ocean waves and water physics that were groundbreaking for animation.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the animation technique used for the hair in Rapunzel in Tangled?

questions.prompt: What was the first Disney film to use 3D animation for characters?
questions.fact: Beauty and the Beast was the first Disney film to use 3D computer animation for characters and backgrounds, particularly in the ballroom scene.

questions.prompt: What animation technique did Disney use for the characters in The Princess and the Frog?
questions.fact: The Princess and the Frog, released in 2009, returned to traditional hand-drawn animation, marking a comeback for 2D animation at Disney.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the animation technique used for the snow in Frozen?
questions.fact: Frozen used advanced computer-generated imagery for the snow and ice effects, creating realistic snowflakes and ice particles that were unique to each scene.

questions.prompt: What animation technique did Disney use for the characters in Big Hero 6?
questions.fact: Big Hero 6, released in 2014, used computer-generated imagery for all characters and environments, creating a unique blend of 2D and 3D animation styles.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the animation technique used for the animals in The Lion King (1994)?
questions.fact: The Lion King (1994) used traditional hand-drawn animation for all characters. Animators studied real animals to create realistic movements and behaviors.

questions.prompt: What animation technique did Disney use for the characters in Encanto?
questions.fact: Encanto, released in 2021, used computer-generated imagery for all characters and environments, creating a vibrant and magical world inspired by Colombian culture.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the animation technique used for the characters in Raya and the Last Dragon?
questions.fact: Raya and the Last Dragon used computer-generated imagery with a unique watercolor-inspired style, creating a visually stunning Southeast Asian-inspired world.

questions.prompt: What animation technique did Disney use for the characters in Wreck-It Ralph?
questions.fact: Wreck-It Ralph, released in 2012, used computer-generated imagery to create different animation styles for different video game worlds, from 8-bit to modern 3D.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the animation technique used for the characters in Zootopia?
questions.fact: Zootopia, released in 2016, used computer-generated imagery to create a diverse city of anthropomorphic animals, each with unique fur textures and characteristics.

questions.prompt: What animation technique did Disney use for the characters in The Incredibles?
questions.fact: The Incredibles, released in 2004, used computer-generated imagery and was produced by Pixar. It featured stylized human characters with superhero abilities.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the iconic ride at Disneyland that takes you through 'it's a small world'?

questions.prompt: What is the name of the roller coaster in the dark at Disneyland?

questions.prompt: What is the name of the ride based on pirates at Disneyland?

questions.prompt: What is the name of the ride based on Star Wars at Disney's Hollywood Studios?

questions.fact: Mickey Mouse doesn't have a mouse friend, but he has many other animal friends including Goofy, Donald Duck, and Pluto.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the character who is known for his temper?

questions.prompt: When was The Walt Disney Company founded?

questions.prompt: What was the original name of The Walt Disney Company?
questions.fact: The company was originally called Disney Brothers Studio when it was founded in 1923. It was later renamed Walt Disney Productions and then The Walt Disney Company.

questions.prompt: What year did Disney acquire Pixar?
questions.fact: Disney acquired Pixar in 2006 for $7.4 billion. This brought together two of the most successful animation studios in history.

questions.prompt: What year did Disney acquire Marvel?

questions.prompt: What year did Disney acquire Lucasfilm?

questions.prompt: What year did Disney acquire 21st Century Fox?

questions.prompt: What is the name of Disney's streaming service?

questions.prompt: What year did Disney+ launch?

questions.prompt: What is the name of Disney's cable television network?

questions.prompt: What is the name of Disney's cruise line?

questions.prompt: What is the name of Disney's publishing division?

questions.prompt: What is the name of Disney's record label?

questions.prompt: What is the name of Disney's video game division?

questions.prompt: What is the name of Disney's consumer products division?

questions.prompt: What is the name of Disney's theatrical production division?

questions.prompt: What is the name of Disney's first Broadway show?

questions.prompt: What is the name of Disney's longest-running Broadway show?

questions.prompt: What is the name of Disney's first theme park?

questions.prompt: What is the name of Disney's largest theme park resort?

questions.prompt: When was The Walt Disney Company founded?

questions.prompt: What was the name of Walt Disney's first successful cartoon character?

questions.prompt: What was the name of Mickey Mouse's first cartoon?

questions.prompt: What year was Mickey Mouse created?
questions.fact: Mickey Mouse was created in 1928 by Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks. He made his debut in Steamboat Willie on November 18, 1928.

questions.prompt: What was the name of Walt Disney's first full-length animated feature?
options: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
questions.fact: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, released in 1937, was Walt Disney's first full-length animated feature. It was a huge risk but became a massive success.

questions.prompt: What year did Walt Disney die?
questions.fact: Walt Disney died on December 15, 1966, from lung cancer. He was 65 years old and never saw Walt Disney World completed.

questions.prompt: What was the name of Walt Disney's brother who co-founded the company?
questions.fact: Roy O. Disney was Walt's older brother and business partner. He co-founded the Disney Brothers Studio and later became the company's CEO after Walt's death.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the first Disney television show?
options: Walt Disney's Wonderful World of Color

questions.prompt: What causes earthquakes?
questions.fact: Earthquakes are caused by the movement of tectonic plates, the massive slabs of rock that make up Earth's crust. When plates move past each other, they can get stuck and then suddenly release energy.

questions.prompt: What instrument measures earthquakes?
questions.fact: A seismograph (or seismometer) measures and records ground motion during earthquakes. The record it produces is called a seismogram.

questions.prompt: What scale measures earthquake magnitude?
questions.fact: The Richter Scale, developed in 1935, measures earthquake magnitude. The Moment Magnitude Scale (Mw) is now more commonly used by seismologists.

questions.prompt: What is the point on Earth's surface directly above where an earthquake starts?
questions.fact: The epicenter is the point on Earth's surface directly above the focus (hypocenter), where the earthquake actually begins underground.

questions.prompt: What is the Ring of Fire?
options: A region with many earthquakes and volcanoes
questions.fact: The Ring of Fire is a region around the Pacific Ocean where many earthquakes and volcanic eruptions occur, due to tectonic plate boundaries and subduction zones.

questions.prompt: What is a tsunami?
questions.fact: A tsunami is a series of large ocean waves caused by earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, or landslides under the ocean. The word means 'harbor wave' in Japanese.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the famous fault line in California?
questions.fact: The San Andreas Fault is a major fault line in California where the Pacific and North American plates meet. It's responsible for many earthquakes in the region.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest earthquake ever recorded?
questions.fact: The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile is the strongest earthquake ever recorded, with a magnitude of 9.5. It caused a devastating tsunami that affected the entire Pacific.

questions.prompt: What are aftershocks?
options: Smaller earthquakes after a main earthquake
Larger earthquakes after a main earthquake
questions.fact: Aftershocks are smaller earthquakes that occur after a main earthquake, as the Earth's crust adjusts to the changes caused by the main quake. They can continue for days, weeks, or even months.

questions.prompt: What percentage of earthquakes occur along the Ring of Fire?
questions.fact: About 90% of the world's earthquakes occur along the Ring of Fire, a horseshoe-shaped zone around the Pacific Ocean where many tectonic plate boundaries meet.

questions.prompt: What is ecology?
options: Study of interactions between organisms and environment
questions.fact: Ecology is the study of how organisms interact with each other and their environment.

questions.prompt: What is an ecosystem?
options: A community of living and non-living things
questions.fact: An ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with their physical environment.

questions.prompt: What is a food chain?
options: A sequence of who eats whom
questions.fact: A food chain shows the sequence of who eats whom in an ecosystem, transferring energy.

questions.prompt: What is a producer?
options: An organism that makes its own food
questions.fact: Producers, like plants, make their own food through photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: What is a consumer?
options: An organism that eats other organisms
questions.fact: Consumers are organisms that eat other organisms for energy.

questions.prompt: What is a decomposer?
options: An organism that breaks down dead matter
questions.fact: Decomposers, like bacteria and fungi, break down dead organic matter and return nutrients to the soil.

questions.prompt: What is biodiversity?
options: Variety of life in an area
questions.fact: Biodiversity refers to the variety of life forms in a particular habitat or ecosystem.

questions.prompt: What is a habitat?
options: The natural environment where an organism lives
questions.fact: A habitat is the natural environment where an organism lives and finds what it needs to survive.

questions.prompt: What is a niche?
options: An organism's role in its ecosystem
questions.fact: A niche is an organism's role in its ecosystem, including what it eats and how it interacts with other species.

questions.prompt: What is a population?
options: A group of the same species in an area
questions.fact: A population is a group of individuals of the same species living in the same area.

questions.prompt: What is a community?
questions.fact: A community consists of all the different populations of species living in the same area.

questions.prompt: What is photosynthesis?
questions.fact: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants convert sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide into glucose and oxygen.

questions.prompt: What is a predator?
options: An organism that hunts and eats other organisms
questions.fact: A predator is an organism that hunts and kills other organisms for food.

questions.prompt: What is prey?
options: An organism that is hunted and eaten
questions.fact: Prey are organisms that are hunted and eaten by predators.

questions.prompt: What is symbiosis?
questions.fact: Symbiosis is a close, long-term relationship between different species, which can be mutualistic, parasitic, or commensal.

questions.prompt: What is mutualism?
questions.fact: Mutualism is a type of symbiosis where both species benefit from the relationship.

questions.prompt: What is competition?
questions.fact: Competition occurs when organisms struggle for the same limited resources like food, water, or space.

questions.prompt: What is a food web?
questions.fact: A food web is a complex network of interconnected food chains showing all feeding relationships in an ecosystem.

questions.prompt: What is carrying capacity?
questions.fact: Carrying capacity is the maximum number of individuals an environment can support sustainably.

questions.prompt: What is the study of ecosystems called?
questions.fact: Ecology is the scientific study of interactions between organisms and their environment.

questions.prompt: What is an ecosystem?
options: A community of living things and their environment
questions.fact: An ecosystem is a community of living organisms (plants, animals, and microbes) interacting with their physical environment (air, water, soil) in a specific area.

questions.prompt: What are the living parts of an ecosystem called?
questions.fact: The living parts of an ecosystem are called biotic factors. These include all plants, animals, fungi, and microorganisms.

questions.prompt: What are the non-living parts of an ecosystem called?
questions.fact: The non-living parts of an ecosystem are called abiotic factors. These include sunlight, water, air, soil, temperature, and minerals.

questions.prompt: What is a producer?
options: An animal that eats other animals
An organism that makes its own food
An organism that breaks down dead things
questions.fact: A producer is an organism that makes its own food, usually through photosynthesis. Plants are the main producers in most ecosystems.

questions.prompt: What is a consumer?
options: An organism that makes its own food
An organism that eats other organisms
An organism that breaks down dead things
questions.fact: A consumer is an organism that eats other organisms to get energy. Consumers include herbivores (plant-eaters), carnivores (meat-eaters), and omnivores (both).

questions.prompt: What is a food chain?
options: The path energy takes through an ecosystem
questions.fact: A food chain shows the path energy takes through an ecosystem, from producers to consumers. For example: grass → rabbit → fox.

questions.prompt: What is a food web?
questions.fact: A food web is multiple interconnected food chains, showing how energy flows through an ecosystem. It's more complex and realistic than a single food chain.

questions.prompt: What is a decomposer?
options: An organism that makes its own food
An organism that eats other organisms
An organism that breaks down dead things
questions.fact: A decomposer is an organism that breaks down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil. Examples include bacteria, fungi, and earthworms.

questions.prompt: What happens if one part of an ecosystem is removed?
options: It can affect the entire ecosystem
questions.fact: If one part of an ecosystem is removed, it can affect the entire ecosystem because all parts are interconnected. This is why biodiversity and conservation are important.

questions.prompt: What is biodiversity?
options: The number of one type of organism
The variety of life in an ecosystem
questions.fact: Biodiversity is the variety of life in an ecosystem, including the number of different species and the genetic diversity within species. High biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable.

questions.prompt: What is the basic emotion that involves feeling good?
questions.fact: Happiness is a positive emotion that involves feeling good, content, or joyful. It's one of the most sought-after emotions and is important for overall well-being.

questions.prompt: What emotion is associated with danger or threat?
questions.fact: Fear is an emotion associated with danger or threat. It's a survival mechanism that helps us respond to dangerous situations by fighting, fleeing, or freezing.

questions.prompt: What are the six basic emotions?
options: Happy, sad, angry, scared, surprised, disgusted
Happy, sad, mad, afraid, shocked, grossed out
The Battle of the Somme (World War I)
questions.fact: The six basic emotions, identified by psychologist Paul Ekman, are happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, and disgust. These are recognized across cultures.

questions.prompt: What emotion is often shown with a smile?
questions.fact: Happiness is often shown with a smile. Smiling can actually trigger the release of neurotransmitters like dopamine and serotonin, making you feel happier.

questions.prompt: What emotion involves feeling sorry or regretful?
questions.fact: Guilt and shame are emotions that involve feeling sorry or regretful about something. Guilt is about actions, while shame is about the self.

questions.prompt: What emotion is the opposite of happiness?
questions.fact: Sadness is often considered the opposite of happiness. It's a natural emotion that helps us process loss and difficult situations.

questions.prompt: What emotion involves feeling excited or eager?
options: The Battle of the Somme (World War I)
questions.fact: Excitement is an emotion that involves feeling thrilled, eager, or enthusiastic about something. It's a positive emotion that can be energizing.

questions.prompt: What is empathy?
questions.fact: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others. It's an important social skill that helps us connect with and help others.

questions.prompt: What emotion involves feeling proud of yourself?
questions.fact: Pride is an emotion that involves feeling satisfied and pleased with yourself or your achievements. It's a positive emotion that can boost self-esteem.

questions.prompt: Can emotions be controlled?
questions.fact: While we can't completely control our emotions, we can learn to manage them through awareness, mindfulness, and practice. This is called emotional regulation.

questions.prompt: What is energy?
questions.fact: Energy is the ability to do work or cause change. It exists in many forms, including kinetic (motion), potential (stored), thermal (heat), and chemical energy.

questions.prompt: What is kinetic energy?
questions.fact: Kinetic energy is the energy an object possesses due to its motion. The faster an object moves, the more kinetic energy it has.

questions.prompt: What is potential energy?
questions.fact: Potential energy is stored energy that an object has because of its position or condition. Examples include a ball at the top of a hill or a stretched spring.

questions.prompt: What is the law of conservation of energy?
options: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed
questions.fact: The law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one form to another. This is a fundamental law of physics.

questions.prompt: What is the main source of energy on Earth?
questions.fact: The Sun is the main source of energy on Earth. It provides light and heat that drive weather, grow plants, and power many natural processes.

questions.prompt: What is renewable energy?
options: Energy that can be used up
questions.fact: Renewable energy is energy from sources that can be replenished naturally, such as solar, wind, hydroelectric, and geothermal energy.

questions.prompt: What is solar energy?
questions.fact: Solar energy is energy from the Sun, captured using solar panels that convert sunlight into electricity. It's a clean, renewable source of energy.

questions.prompt: What is the unit of energy?
questions.fact: The joule is the standard unit of energy in the metric system. It's named after James Prescott Joule, who studied energy and heat.

questions.prompt: What is the most efficient form of energy?
options: There is no single most efficient form
questions.fact: Energy efficiency depends on many factors. Nuclear energy is very efficient for electricity generation, while solar and wind are efficient for renewable energy. The 'best' depends on the application.

questions.prompt: What happens to energy when you use it?
options: It is transformed into other forms
questions.fact: When energy is used, it's transformed into other forms. For example, chemical energy in food becomes kinetic energy when you move, and some becomes heat energy.
