questions.prompt: What was the name of the period after the fall of the Roman Empire?
questions.fact: The Middle Ages (also called the Medieval Period) lasted from about 500 to 1500 AD. It began after the fall of the Western Roman Empire.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Frankish king who was crowned Holy Roman Emperor?
questions.fact: Charlemagne (Charles the Great) was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 800 AD by Pope Leo III. He united much of Western Europe and promoted learning and culture.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the series of religious wars to reclaim the Holy Land?
questions.fact: The Crusades were a series of religious wars from 1096 to 1291 where European Christians tried to reclaim the Holy Land from Muslim control.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the plague that killed millions in the 14th century?
questions.fact: The Black Death (bubonic plague) killed an estimated 75-200 million people in Europe and Asia in the 14th century, reducing Europe's population by 30-60%.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the war between England and France that lasted over 100 years?
questions.fact: The Hundred Years' War (1337-1453) was a series of conflicts between England and France over the French throne. It actually lasted 116 years.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the English civil war between two royal houses?
questions.fact: The War of the Roses (1455-1487) was a civil war between the House of Lancaster (red rose) and the House of York (white rose) for the English throne.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the period of cultural and intellectual revival in Europe?
questions.fact: The Renaissance (14th-17th centuries) was a period of cultural and intellectual revival in Europe. It began in Italy and spread throughout Europe.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the movement that split Western Christianity?
questions.fact: The Protestant Reformation (1517-1648) split Western Christianity into Catholic and Protestant branches. It was started by Martin Luther's 95 Theses.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the war fought over religion in the 17th century?
questions.fact: The Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) was fought primarily in Central Europe over religion and territory. It was one of the most destructive wars in European history.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the period of intellectual and philosophical movement?
questions.fact: The Enlightenment (17th-18th centuries) was a period of intellectual and philosophical movement that emphasized reason, science, and individual rights.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the French Revolution?
questions.fact: The French Revolution began in 1789 with the storming of the Bastille. It led to the overthrow of the monarchy and the rise of Napoleon Bonaparte.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the French emperor who conquered much of Europe?
questions.fact: Napoleon Bonaparte (1769-1821) was a French military leader who became emperor and conquered much of Europe. He was finally defeated at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the battle where Napoleon was finally defeated?
questions.fact: The Battle of Waterloo (1815) was Napoleon's final defeat. He was defeated by a coalition of British, Prussian, and other European forces.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the period of rapid industrialization?
questions.fact: The Industrial Revolution (18th-19th centuries) was a period of rapid industrialization that transformed Europe and the world. It began in Britain and spread throughout Europe.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the war fought between Russia and several European powers?
questions.fact: The Crimean War (1853-1856) was fought between Russia and an alliance of Britain, France, the Ottoman Empire, and Sardinia. It was one of the first 'modern' wars.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the unification of Germany?
questions.fact: Germany was unified in 1871 under the leadership of Otto von Bismarck. The German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the unification of Italy?
questions.fact: Italy was unified in 1861 under the leadership of figures like Giuseppe Garibaldi and Count Camillo di Cavour. The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the war that began World War I?
options: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
questions.fact: World War I began in 1914 after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary. This triggered a chain of events that led to war.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the treaty that ended World War I?
questions.fact: The Treaty of Versailles, signed in 1919, officially ended World War I. It imposed harsh penalties on Germany and is often cited as a cause of World War II.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Spanish Civil War?
questions.fact: The Spanish Civil War (1936-1939) was fought between the Republican government and Nationalist forces led by Francisco Franco. It was a prelude to World War II.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the fall of the Berlin Wall?
questions.fact: The Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, marking the end of the Cold War and the reunification of Germany. It had divided East and West Berlin for 28 years.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the dissolution of the Soviet Union?
questions.fact: The Soviet Union was dissolved in 1991, ending the Cold War. This led to the independence of 15 former Soviet republics and the end of communist rule in Eastern Europe.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the European Union?
questions.fact: The European Union evolved from the European Economic Community (EEC), which was created in 1957. It became the European Union in 1993 with the Maastricht Treaty.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the British prime minister during World War II?
questions.fact: Winston Churchill was the British prime minister during most of World War II. He led Britain through its darkest hours and inspired the nation with his speeches.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the French general who led the Free French Forces?
questions.fact: Charles de Gaulle led the Free French Forces during World War II and later became president of France. He is considered one of France's greatest leaders.

questions.prompt: Who proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection?
questions.fact: Charles Darwin published 'On the Origin of Species' in 1859, introducing the theory of evolution by natural selection.

questions.prompt: What is natural selection?
questions.fact: Natural selection is the process where organisms better adapted to their environment tend to survive and produce more offspring.

questions.prompt: How old is the Earth approximately?
questions.fact: Earth is approximately 4.5 billion years old, giving plenty of time for evolution to occur.

questions.prompt: What is a fossil?
questions.fact: Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of ancient organisms, providing evidence of evolution.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest unit of evolution?
questions.fact: Populations, not individuals, evolve. Evolution is the change in allele frequencies in a population over time.

questions.prompt: What is speciation?
questions.fact: Speciation is the evolutionary process by which populations evolve to become distinct species.

questions.prompt: What is a common ancestor?
options: An extinct species from which two or more species evolved
questions.fact: A common ancestor is an ancestral species from which two or more descendant species evolved.

questions.prompt: What evidence supports evolution?
questions.fact: Evolution is supported by multiple lines of evidence including fossils, DNA similarities, comparative anatomy, and embryology.

questions.prompt: What is adaptive radiation?
questions.fact: Adaptive radiation is the rapid evolution of many diverse species from a common ancestor, often after a major environmental change.

questions.prompt: What is genetic drift?
questions.fact: Genetic drift is the random change in allele frequencies in a population, especially in small populations.

questions.prompt: What is convergent evolution?
questions.fact: Convergent evolution occurs when unrelated species independently evolve similar traits due to similar environmental pressures.

questions.prompt: What is the origin of life called?
questions.fact: Abiogenesis is the natural process by which life arises from non-living matter, distinct from evolution which is the change in existing life.

questions.prompt: What is a vestigial structure?
options: A structure with no current function
questions.fact: Vestigial structures are anatomical features that have lost their original function through evolution, like the human appendix.

questions.prompt: What is coevolution?
questions.fact: Coevolution occurs when two or more species reciprocally affect each other's evolution, like flowers and their pollinators.

questions.prompt: What is the molecular clock?
options: Using DNA mutations to estimate evolutionary time
questions.fact: The molecular clock uses the rate of genetic mutations to estimate when species diverged from common ancestors.

questions.prompt: What is punctuated equilibrium?
options: Long periods of stability with rapid change
questions.fact: Punctuated equilibrium suggests evolution occurs in rapid bursts separated by long periods of stability.

questions.prompt: What is homology?
questions.fact: Homology refers to similar structures in different species that share a common evolutionary origin, like the forelimbs of mammals.

questions.prompt: What is the endosymbiotic theory?
questions.fact: The endosymbiotic theory explains how mitochondria and chloroplasts evolved from bacteria that were engulfed by early cells.

questions.prompt: What is microevolution?
questions.fact: Microevolution refers to small-scale changes in allele frequencies within a population over a few generations.

questions.prompt: What is macroevolution?
options: Large-scale evolutionary changes over long periods
questions.fact: Macroevolution refers to large-scale evolutionary changes that occur over long periods, including speciation and extinction events.

questions.prompt: Who is credited with discovering America?
questions.fact: While Christopher Columbus is often credited with 'discovering' America in 1492, Leif Erikson reached North America around 1000 CE, and the continent is named after Amerigo Vespucci.

questions.prompt: Who was the first person to circumnavigate the globe?
questions.fact: Ferdinand Magellan's expedition (1519-1522) was the first to circumnavigate the globe, though Magellan himself died in the Philippines. Only one of his five ships completed the journey.

questions.prompt: Who explored the Mississippi River?
questions.fact: Multiple explorers explored the Mississippi River: Marquette and Joliet in 1673, La Salle who claimed it for France in 1682, and Lewis and Clark who explored its upper reaches.

questions.prompt: Who was the first European to reach India by sea?
questions.fact: Vasco da Gama was the first European to reach India by sea in 1498, establishing a sea route from Europe to Asia and opening the way for European colonialism.

questions.prompt: Who explored the Pacific Northwest?
questions.fact: Lewis and Clark explored the Pacific Northwest from 1804-1806, commissioned by President Thomas Jefferson to find a route to the Pacific Ocean.

questions.prompt: Who was the first person to reach the South Pole?
questions.fact: Roald Amundsen was the first person to reach the South Pole on December 14, 1911, beating Robert Falcon Scott's expedition by about a month.

questions.prompt: Who was the first person to reach the North Pole?
questions.fact: Robert Peary claimed to be the first person to reach the North Pole on April 6, 1909, though his claim has been disputed. Frederick Cook also claimed to have reached it first.

questions.prompt: Who was the first European to see the Pacific Ocean from the Americas?
questions.fact: Vasco Núñez de Balboa was the first European to see the Pacific Ocean from the Americas in 1513, after crossing the Isthmus of Panama.

questions.prompt: Who explored the interior of Africa?
questions.fact: David Livingstone, Henry Stanley, and Mungo Park were all famous African explorers. Stanley famously found Livingstone with the words 'Dr. Livingstone, I presume?'

questions.prompt: Who was the first person to climb Mount Everest?
options: The Battle of the Somme (World War I)
questions.fact: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay were the first people to successfully reach the summit of Mount Everest on May 29, 1953, as part of a British expedition.

questions.prompt: What is the largest living fish species?
questions.fact: The whale shark is the largest living fish. Blue whales are larger, but they are mammals.

questions.prompt: How do most bony fish obtain oxygen from water?

questions.prompt: What is the fastest fish in the ocean?

questions.prompt: What percentage of a fish's body is water?
questions.fact: Fish are composed of about 80% water, similar to the water content of the ocean they live in. This helps maintain their internal balance.

questions.prompt: What is the name for a group of fish?

questions.prompt: What is the smallest fish in the world?

questions.prompt: How many hearts does a fish have?
questions.fact: Fish have one heart, just like humans. Their heart pumps blood through their gills to get oxygen and then throughout their body.

questions.prompt: What is the most common fish in the ocean?
questions.fact: The bristlemouth is the most common fish in the ocean, with billions of them in the deep sea. They're small, bioluminescent fish that live in the twilight zone.

questions.prompt: What is a fish without a jaw called?
questions.fact: Jawless fish, like lampreys and hagfish, are primitive fish that don't have jaws. They're the most ancient group of vertebrates.

questions.prompt: Can fish see in color?
options: No, they only see in black and white
Yes, most fish can see colors
Only some fish can see colors
questions.fact: Most fish can see colors, and many have better color vision than humans. Some fish can even see ultraviolet light, which humans cannot see.

questions.prompt: Which country's flag has horizontal stripes of orange, white, and green?

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of flowers?
questions.fact: The main purpose of flowers is to produce seeds through reproduction. While flowers may look pretty and attract pollinators, their primary function is reproduction.

questions.prompt: What is the largest flower in the world?

questions.prompt: What is the national flower of the United States?

questions.prompt: What do bees get from flowers?

questions.fact: Bees get both nectar (a sweet liquid) and pollen (protein-rich powder) from flowers. Nectar is used to make honey, and pollen is food for bee larvae.

questions.prompt: What is the process called when pollen is transferred from one flower to another?
questions.fact: Pollination is the process by which pollen is transferred from the male part of a flower to the female part, allowing fertilization and seed production.

questions.prompt: What flower is known for following the sun?
questions.fact: Sunflowers are known for heliotropism - they turn their flowers to face the sun as it moves across the sky during the day.

questions.prompt: What is the most common flower color?
questions.fact: Yellow is one of the most common flower colors in nature, as it's highly visible to pollinators like bees, which can see yellow well.

questions.prompt: What flower is associated with Valentine's Day?
questions.fact: Roses, especially red roses, are associated with Valentine's Day and are a traditional symbol of love and romance.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest flower in the world?

questions.prompt: How many petals do most flowers have?

questions.prompt: What is the process of cooking food in hot oil called?
questions.fact: Frying is the cooking method where food is cooked in hot oil or fat. There are different types: shallow frying, deep frying, and stir-frying.

questions.prompt: What is the main ingredient in paella?

questions.prompt: What is the process of preserving food by removing water called?
questions.fact: Dehydration (or drying) is a food preservation method that removes water from food, inhibiting the growth of microorganisms. Examples include dried fruits, jerky, and herbs.

questions.prompt: What is a force?
questions.fact: A force is a push or pull that can cause an object to move, stop, or change direction. Forces are measured in newtons (N).

questions.prompt: What is gravity?
options: A force that pulls objects toward each other
A force that pushes objects apart
questions.fact: Gravity is a force that pulls objects toward each other. On Earth, gravity pulls objects toward the ground, giving them weight.

questions.prompt: What is the acceleration due to gravity on Earth?
questions.fact: The acceleration due to gravity on Earth is approximately 9.8 m/s², meaning objects fall faster by 9.8 meters per second every second they fall.

questions.prompt: What is friction?
questions.fact: Friction is a force that opposes motion between two surfaces in contact. It can be helpful (like when walking) or a hindrance (like when trying to move heavy objects).

questions.prompt: What is Newton's first law of motion?
options: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction
An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion
Energy cannot be created or destroyed
questions.fact: Newton's first law states that an object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at a constant velocity, unless acted upon by an unbalanced force. This is also called the law of inertia.

questions.prompt: What is Newton's second law of motion?
options: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction
An object at rest stays at rest
questions.fact: Newton's second law states that force equals mass times acceleration (F = ma). This means the greater the force, the greater the acceleration, or the greater the mass, the less the acceleration.

questions.prompt: What is Newton's third law of motion?
options: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction
An object at rest stays at rest
questions.fact: Newton's third law states that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. For example, when you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you with equal force.

questions.prompt: What is magnetism?
questions.fact: Magnetism is a force between magnetic objects. Magnets have north and south poles, and like poles repel while opposite poles attract.

questions.prompt: What is the unit of force?
questions.fact: The newton (N) is the unit of force, named after Isaac Newton. One newton is the force needed to accelerate one kilogram of mass by one meter per second squared.

questions.prompt: What happens when forces are balanced?
options: The object doesn't move or moves at constant speed
questions.fact: When forces are balanced (equal and opposite), the object either doesn't move or moves at a constant speed. Unbalanced forces cause acceleration.

questions.prompt: What was the French Revolution?
options: A period of radical change in France
questions.fact: The French Revolution (1789-1799) was a period of radical political and social change in France.

questions.prompt: What was the Bastille?
questions.fact: The Bastille was a prison fortress in Paris, and its storming on July 14, 1789, marked the start of the revolution.

questions.prompt: What was the motto of the French Revolution?
questions.fact: 'Liberty, Equality, Fraternity' (Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité) was the motto of the French Revolution.

questions.prompt: What was the Reign of Terror?
questions.fact: The Reign of Terror (1793-1794) was a period of mass executions during the revolution, led by Robespierre.

questions.prompt: What was the guillotine?
questions.fact: The guillotine was a device used for executions during the revolution, designed to be a more humane method.

questions.prompt: What was the study of the French Revolution called?
questions.fact: The French Revolution is studied through history, political science, and revolutionary studies.

questions.prompt: What was the period of the French Revolution?
questions.fact: The French Revolution lasted from 1789 to 1799, ending with Napoleon's rise to power.

questions.prompt: What was the Estates-General?

questions.prompt: What was the Third Estate?
questions.fact: The Third Estate was the commoners (peasants, workers, bourgeoisie), who made up 98% of the population.

questions.prompt: What was the National Assembly?
questions.fact: The National Assembly was formed by the Third Estate, declaring itself the true representative of France.

questions.prompt: What was the Declaration of the Rights of Man?
questions.fact: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789) declared fundamental rights and principles.

questions.prompt: What was Louis XVI?
options: The king executed during the revolution
questions.fact: Louis XVI was the king of France who was executed by guillotine in 1793 during the revolution.

questions.prompt: What was Marie Antoinette?
options: The queen executed during the revolution
questions.fact: Marie Antoinette was the queen of France, executed by guillotine in 1793, famous for saying 'Let them eat cake.'

questions.prompt: What was Robespierre?
questions.fact: Maximilien Robespierre was a revolutionary leader who led the Reign of Terror before being executed himself.

questions.prompt: What was the impact of the French Revolution?
options: Ended the monarchy and transformed France
questions.fact: The French Revolution ended the monarchy, established a republic, and had profound effects on France and Europe.

questions.prompt: What was the Directory?
questions.fact: The Directory was the government that ruled France from 1795 to 1799, before Napoleon's rise.

questions.prompt: What was the impact on Europe?
questions.fact: The French Revolution inspired revolutions across Europe and led to the Napoleonic Wars.

questions.prompt: What was the storming of the Bastille?
options: The event that started the revolution
questions.fact: The storming of the Bastille on July 14, 1789, is considered the start of the French Revolution.

questions.prompt: What was the significance of the French Revolution?
options: Marked the end of absolute monarchy
questions.fact: The French Revolution marked the end of absolute monarchy in France and the rise of modern democracy.

questions.prompt: What was the role of the peasants?

questions.prompt: How many seasons are there?
questions.fact: There are four seasons: spring, summer, fall (autumn), and winter. The seasons are caused by Earth's tilt on its axis as it orbits the Sun.

questions.prompt: What causes the seasons?
questions.fact: Seasons are caused by Earth's tilt on its axis (about 23.5 degrees) as it orbits the Sun, not by Earth's distance from the Sun. When the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, it's summer there.

questions.prompt: What is the first day of summer in the Northern Hemisphere called?
questions.fact: The summer solstice (around June 21) is the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere, when the North Pole is tilted closest to the Sun.

questions.prompt: What is the first day of spring called?
questions.fact: The vernal (spring) equinox (around March 20-21) marks the first day of spring, when day and night are approximately equal in length.

questions.prompt: Which season has the shortest days?
questions.fact: Winter has the shortest days because the hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun. The winter solstice (around December 21) is the shortest day of the year.

questions.prompt: What season comes after summer?
questions.fact: Fall (autumn) comes after summer. In the Northern Hemisphere, fall typically runs from September to November, marked by cooler temperatures and falling leaves.

questions.prompt: What is the name for when day and night are equal in length?
questions.fact: An equinox occurs when day and night are approximately equal in length. There are two equinoxes each year: the vernal (spring) and autumnal (fall) equinoxes.

questions.prompt: Which season is known for blooming flowers?
questions.fact: Spring is known for blooming flowers as plants come back to life after winter. Many plants flower in spring to take advantage of increasing daylight and warmer temperatures.

questions.prompt: What is the warmest season?
questions.fact: Summer is typically the warmest season because the hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, receiving more direct sunlight and longer days.

questions.prompt: What season is associated with falling leaves?
questions.fact: Fall (autumn) is associated with falling leaves as trees prepare for winter by dropping their leaves. The changing colors of leaves are caused by the breakdown of chlorophyll.

questions.prompt: What causes the seasons?
questions.fact: Seasons are caused by Earth's tilt on its axis (about 23.5 degrees) as it orbits the Sun, not by Earth's distance from the Sun. When the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, it's summer there.

questions.prompt: What is the summer solstice?
options: The shortest day of the year
The longest day of the year
When day and night are equal
questions.fact: The summer solstice (around June 21 in the Northern Hemisphere) is the longest day of the year, when the Sun is at its highest point in the sky.

questions.prompt: What is the winter solstice?
options: The longest day of the year
The shortest day of the year
When day and night are equal
questions.fact: The winter solstice (around December 21 in the Northern Hemisphere) is the shortest day of the year, when the Sun is at its lowest point in the sky.

questions.prompt: What is an equinox?
options: The longest day of the year
The shortest day of the year
When day and night are approximately equal
The hottest day of the year
questions.fact: An equinox occurs when day and night are approximately equal in length. There are two equinoxes each year: the vernal (spring) and autumnal (fall) equinoxes.

questions.prompt: When is the vernal equinox?
questions.fact: The vernal (spring) equinox occurs around March 20-21 in the Northern Hemisphere, marking the first day of spring when day and night are equal.

questions.prompt: When is the autumnal equinox?
questions.fact: The autumnal (fall) equinox occurs around September 22-23 in the Northern Hemisphere, marking the first day of fall when day and night are equal.

questions.prompt: What season is it in the Southern Hemisphere when it's summer in the Northern Hemisphere?
questions.fact: Seasons are opposite in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. When it's summer in the Northern Hemisphere, it's winter in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.prompt: How long does it take Earth to orbit the Sun?
questions.fact: Earth takes approximately 365.25 days to orbit the Sun once. This is why we have a leap year every 4 years to account for the extra quarter day.

questions.prompt: What is the angle of Earth's tilt?
questions.fact: Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5 degrees relative to its orbit around the Sun. This tilt is what causes the seasons.

questions.prompt: Do all places on Earth have four seasons?
options: No, some places have only wet and dry seasons
questions.fact: Not all places have four distinct seasons. Places near the equator have little seasonal variation, while some tropical regions have wet and dry seasons instead of spring, summer, fall, and winter.

questions.prompt: How many senses do humans have?

questions.prompt: What are the five traditional senses?
options: The Battle of the Somme (World War I)
questions.fact: The five traditional senses are sight (vision), hearing (sound), taste (flavor), smell (scent), and touch (feeling). These are the basic ways we perceive the world.

questions.prompt: What organ is used for sight?
questions.fact: The eyes are the organs used for sight. They detect light and convert it into electrical signals that the brain interprets as images.

questions.prompt: What organ is used for hearing?
questions.fact: The ears are the organs used for hearing. They detect sound waves and convert them into electrical signals that the brain interprets as sounds.

questions.prompt: What organ is used for taste?
questions.fact: The tongue is the organ primarily used for taste, with taste buds that can detect five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami.

questions.prompt: What organ is used for smell?
questions.fact: The nose is the organ used for smell. It contains olfactory receptors that detect chemicals in the air and send signals to the brain.

questions.prompt: What is the largest sense organ?
questions.fact: The skin is the largest sense organ, covering the entire body. It's responsible for the sense of touch and also helps detect temperature and pain.

questions.prompt: How many basic tastes can humans detect?

questions.prompt: What sense is closely linked to memory?
questions.fact: Smell is closely linked to memory because the olfactory system is directly connected to the brain's memory and emotion centers. Scents can trigger vivid memories.

questions.prompt: What sense helps us maintain balance?
questions.fact: The vestibular sense (located in the inner ear) helps us maintain balance and sense our body's position and movement in space. It works with vision and proprioception.

questions.prompt: What shape has no sides?
questions.fact: A circle has no sides - it's a curved shape with all points equidistant from the center. It has infinite points but no straight edges.

questions.prompt: What is a shape with 4 sides called?
questions.fact: A quadrilateral is any polygon with 4 sides. Squares, rectangles, parallelograms, and trapezoids are all types of quadrilaterals.

questions.prompt: What shape has all sides equal and all angles equal?
questions.fact: A regular polygon has all sides equal in length and all angles equal in measure. Examples include equilateral triangles, squares, and regular pentagons.

questions.prompt: What is a 3D shape with 6 square faces called?
questions.fact: A cube is a 3D shape with 6 square faces, 12 edges, and 8 vertices. All faces are equal squares, and all edges are equal in length.

questions.prompt: What is a perfectly round 3D shape called?
questions.fact: A sphere is a perfectly round 3D shape where all points on the surface are equidistant from the center. Earth is approximately a sphere.

questions.prompt: What is alpine skiing?
questions.fact: Alpine skiing is downhill skiing on slopes, the most common form of recreational skiing.

questions.prompt: What is cross-country skiing?
options: Skiing across flat or rolling terrain
questions.fact: Cross-country skiing involves skiing across flat or rolling terrain, often for long distances.

questions.prompt: What is a ski lift?
options: A machine that carries skiers uphill
questions.fact: A ski lift is a mechanical device that transports skiers up a mountain to the top of slopes.

questions.prompt: What is a slope?
questions.fact: A slope is an inclined surface on a mountain where skiers descend.

questions.prompt: What is a ski?
options: A long, narrow board for gliding on snow
questions.fact: A ski is a long, narrow board attached to boots that allows gliding on snow.

questions.prompt: What is a ski pole?
options: A stick used for balance and propulsion
questions.fact: Ski poles are sticks used for balance, turning, and propulsion while skiing.

questions.prompt: What is a bunny slope?
questions.fact: A bunny slope is a gentle, easy slope designed for beginners learning to ski.

questions.prompt: What is a black diamond?
questions.fact: A black diamond is the most difficult slope rating, indicating expert-level terrain.

questions.prompt: What is freestyle skiing?
questions.fact: Freestyle skiing involves performing tricks, jumps, and acrobatic maneuvers on skis.

questions.prompt: What is ski jumping?
options: Jumping off a ramp for distance
questions.fact: Ski jumping is a sport where skiers jump off a ramp and are judged on distance and style.

questions.prompt: What is a mogul?
options: A bump on a ski slope
questions.fact: A mogul is a bump formed on a ski slope from repeated turns, creating a challenging terrain.

questions.prompt: What is a chairlift?
questions.fact: A chairlift is a type of ski lift with suspended chairs that carry skiers up the mountain.

questions.prompt: What is a gondola?
questions.fact: A gondola is an enclosed cabin lift that protects skiers from weather while ascending.

questions.prompt: What is parallel skiing?
questions.fact: Parallel skiing is an advanced technique where both skis are kept parallel while turning.

questions.prompt: What is a snowplow?
questions.fact: The snowplow is a beginner technique where skis form a V-shape to slow down or stop.

questions.prompt: What is a ski resort?
options: A facility with slopes and amenities
questions.fact: A ski resort is a facility with multiple slopes, lifts, and amenities for skiing and snowboarding.

questions.prompt: What is backcountry skiing?
questions.fact: Backcountry skiing is skiing in unmarked, ungroomed areas outside of ski resorts.

questions.prompt: What is a ski binding?
options: A device that attaches ski to boot
questions.fact: A ski binding is a device that attaches the ski boot to the ski and releases in a fall.

questions.prompt: What is the study of skiing called?
questions.fact: Skiing is simply called skiing, though it's studied and analyzed by coaches and sports scientists.

questions.prompt: What is a ski instructor?
questions.fact: A ski instructor is a certified teacher who helps people learn and improve their skiing skills.

questions.prompt: How many players are on a soccer team on the field at once?
questions.fact: Each soccer team has 11 players on the field: 1 goalkeeper and 10 outfield players.

questions.prompt: What is the duration of a standard soccer match?
questions.fact: A standard soccer match consists of two 45-minute halves, totaling 90 minutes of play.

questions.prompt: What is the penalty area also called?
questions.fact: The penalty area is commonly called 'the box' or 'the 18-yard box' and is where fouls can result in penalty kicks.

questions.prompt: What is a hat-trick in soccer?
questions.fact: A hat-trick is when a player scores three goals in a single match.

questions.prompt: What is the offside rule?
options: A player ahead of the ball and second-to-last defender
A player in the penalty area
questions.fact: A player is offside if they are ahead of the ball and the second-to-last defender when the ball is played.

questions.prompt: What is the World Cup?
questions.fact: The FIFA World Cup is the most prestigious international soccer tournament, held every four years.

questions.prompt: What is a yellow card?
questions.fact: A yellow card is a caution given to a player for misconduct. Two yellow cards result in a red card.

questions.prompt: What is a red card?
questions.fact: A red card means immediate ejection from the game and the team must play with one fewer player.

questions.prompt: What is the center circle used for?
questions.fact: The center circle is where the game starts at kickoff and after each goal.

questions.prompt: What is a corner kick?
options: A restart when ball goes out over goal line
questions.fact: A corner kick is awarded when the ball goes out of play over the goal line, last touched by the defending team.

questions.prompt: What is the penalty spot distance from goal?
questions.fact: The penalty spot is 12 yards (11 meters) from the goal line.

questions.prompt: What is a free kick?
questions.fact: A free kick is awarded after a foul and can be direct (can score) or indirect (must touch another player first).

questions.prompt: What is the goalkeeper's main role?
questions.fact: The goalkeeper's primary role is to prevent the opposing team from scoring by defending the goal.

questions.prompt: What is extra time?
questions.fact: Extra time consists of two 15-minute periods played when a match is tied after 90 minutes.

questions.prompt: What is a penalty shootout?
questions.fact: A penalty shootout is used to decide a winner when a match is still tied after extra time.

questions.prompt: What is the offside trap?
questions.fact: The offside trap is a defensive tactic where defenders move forward to catch attackers offside.

questions.prompt: What is a nutmeg?
questions.fact: A nutmeg is when a player kicks the ball through an opponent's legs, considered a skillful move.

questions.prompt: What is the Champions League?
questions.fact: The UEFA Champions League is Europe's premier club competition, featuring the best teams from each country.

questions.prompt: What is a bicycle kick?
questions.fact: A bicycle kick is an acrobatic move where a player kicks the ball overhead while in mid-air.

questions.prompt: What is the Golden Boot?
questions.fact: The Golden Boot is awarded to the top goal scorer in a league or tournament.

questions.prompt: What is social media?
options: Online platforms for sharing and interaction
questions.fact: Social media are online platforms that enable users to create, share, and interact with content and other users.

questions.prompt: What was the first major social media platform?
questions.fact: MySpace, launched in 2003, was one of the first major social media platforms, predating Facebook.

questions.prompt: What is Facebook?
questions.fact: Facebook, launched in 2004, is a social networking platform that connects people and allows sharing of content.

questions.prompt: What is Twitter (now X)?
questions.fact: Twitter (now X) is a microblogging platform where users share short messages (originally 140, now 280 characters).

questions.prompt: What is Instagram?
options: A photo and video sharing platform
questions.fact: Instagram is a photo and video sharing platform, launched in 2010, focusing on visual content.

questions.prompt: What is TikTok?
questions.fact: TikTok is a short-form video platform where users create and share videos up to 10 minutes long.

questions.prompt: What is the impact of social media?
questions.fact: Social media has transformed how people communicate, share information, connect, and consume news and entertainment.

questions.prompt: What is a hashtag?
questions.fact: A hashtag is a keyword or phrase preceded by #, used to categorize and find content on social media platforms.

questions.prompt: What is the study of social media called?
questions.fact: Social media is studied through digital media, communication studies, and social media research.

questions.prompt: What is the future of social media?
questions.fact: The future of social media includes new platforms, features, and ways of connecting, with ongoing evolution.

questions.prompt: What is the origin of social media?
questions.fact: Social media emerged in the late 1990s-early 2000s with platforms like Friendster (2002) and MySpace (2003).

questions.prompt: What is a post?
questions.fact: A post is content (text, photo, video) shared on social media platforms for others to see and interact with.

questions.prompt: What is the importance of social media?
options: Major platform for communication and information
questions.fact: Social media has become a major platform for communication, information sharing, business, and social connection.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between social media and traditional media?
options: Social media is interactive and user-generated
questions.fact: Social media is interactive and user-generated, while traditional media (TV, radio, newspapers) is typically one-way communication.

questions.prompt: What is the impact of social media on society?
options: Significant impact on communication, politics, and culture
questions.fact: Social media has significantly impacted communication, politics, business, culture, and how people form relationships.

questions.prompt: What is the importance of privacy on social media?
questions.fact: Privacy on social media is critical for protecting personal information, identity, and safety online.

questions.prompt: What is sound?
questions.fact: Sound is vibrations traveling through a medium (like air, water, or solid objects). When these vibrations reach our ears, we hear sound.

questions.prompt: How does sound travel?
questions.fact: Sound travels in waves, created by vibrations. These waves move through air, water, or other materials, carrying the sound from its source to our ears.

questions.prompt: What is the speed of sound in air?
questions.fact: The speed of sound in air is approximately 343 meters per second (1,125 feet per second) at room temperature, but it varies with temperature and altitude.

questions.prompt: Can sound travel in space?
options: No, there is no air in space
questions.fact: Sound cannot travel in space because there is no air or other medium for the sound waves to travel through. Space is a vacuum, so it's silent.

questions.prompt: What is pitch?
options: How high or low a sound is
questions.fact: Pitch is how high or low a sound is. High-pitched sounds have high frequencies (like a bird chirping), while low-pitched sounds have low frequencies (like a drum).

questions.prompt: What is volume?
options: How high or low a sound is
questions.fact: Volume (or loudness) is how loud a sound is. Loud sounds have high amplitude (bigger waves), while quiet sounds have low amplitude (smaller waves).

questions.prompt: What is an echo?
questions.fact: An echo is a sound that bounces back after hitting a surface. When sound waves hit a hard surface, they reflect back, creating an echo.

questions.prompt: What animal uses echolocation?
questions.fact: Bats use echolocation to navigate and find food. They make high-pitched sounds and listen for the echoes to determine where objects are.

questions.prompt: What is frequency?
options: How many times a sound wave repeats per second
questions.fact: Frequency is how many times a sound wave repeats per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Higher frequency means higher pitch, and lower frequency means lower pitch.

questions.prompt: What is the loudest sound possible?
questions.fact: The loudest possible sound in air is about 194 decibels. Beyond this, the sound wave becomes a shock wave. For comparison, a jet engine is about 140 decibels.

questions.fact: South American countries are studied through geography, Latin American studies, and regional studies.

questions.prompt: What is the importance of South American capitals?
options: Centers of government, culture, and economy
questions.fact: South American capitals are centers of government, culture, economy, and history for their respective countries.

questions.prompt: What is the impact of South American capitals?
options: Major centers of culture and politics
questions.fact: South American capitals are major centers of culture, politics, and economy, influencing their countries and regions.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the first human to walk on the Moon?
questions.fact: Neil Armstrong became the first human to walk on the Moon on July 20, 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission, saying the famous words, 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.'

questions.prompt: What is the name of the first artificial satellite launched into space?
questions.fact: Sputnik 1, launched by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957, was the first artificial satellite, marking the beginning of the space age.

questions.prompt: What is the name of NASA's space telescope launched in 1990?
questions.fact: The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, has revolutionized astronomy by providing stunning images and valuable data about the universe, despite initial technical problems.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the first woman in space?

questions.prompt: What is the name of the planet known as the 'Red Planet'?
questions.fact: Mars is called the 'Red Planet' because of its reddish appearance, caused by iron oxide (rust) on its surface.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the largest moon in our solar system?
questions.fact: Ganymede, one of Jupiter's moons, is the largest moon in our solar system, even larger than the planet Mercury.

questions.prompt: What is a comet primarily made of?
questions.fact: Comets are primarily made of ice, dust, and rocky material. When they approach the Sun, the ice sublimates, creating the characteristic coma and tail.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the first space station?

questions.prompt: What is the name of the force that keeps planets in orbit around the Sun?

questions.prompt: What is the name of the mission that landed the first humans on the Moon?
questions.fact: Apollo 11, launched on July 16, 1969, was the mission that successfully landed the first humans on the Moon, with Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walking on the lunar surface.

questions.prompt: How many players are on a basketball team on the court at one time?
questions.fact: A basketball team has 5 players on the court at one time: typically two guards, two forwards, and one center.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum score in a single turn in bowling?
questions.fact: The maximum score in a single turn in bowling is 30 points, achieved by rolling three consecutive strikes (a turkey).

questions.prompt: How many holes are in a standard round of golf?

questions.prompt: What is the distance of a marathon?
questions.fact: A marathon is exactly 26.2 miles (42.195 kilometers), a distance based on the legend of Pheidippides running from Marathon to Athens in 490 BCE.

questions.prompt: In which sport would you perform a slam dunk?
questions.fact: A slam dunk is a basketball move where a player jumps and forcefully throws the ball downward through the basket, one of the most exciting plays in the sport.

questions.prompt: What is the highest score possible in a single game of tennis?

questions.prompt: In which sport is the term 'home run' used?

questions.prompt: How many periods are in a standard ice hockey game?
questions.fact: A standard ice hockey game consists of three 20-minute periods, with intermissions between periods. Overtime periods are played if the game is tied.

questions.prompt: What is the closest star to Earth?
questions.fact: The Sun is the closest star to Earth, located about 93 million miles (150 million kilometers) away. It's the center of our solar system.

questions.prompt: What is a group of stars that form a pattern called?
questions.fact: A constellation is a group of stars that form a recognizable pattern in the night sky. There are 88 officially recognized constellations.

questions.prompt: What is the brightest star in the night sky?
questions.fact: Sirius, also known as the Dog Star, is the brightest star in the night sky. It's part of the constellation Canis Major and is about 8.6 light-years away.

questions.prompt: What is the North Star?
questions.fact: Polaris, also called the North Star, appears almost directly above Earth's North Pole. It's been used for navigation for thousands of years.

questions.prompt: What color are the hottest stars?
questions.fact: Blue stars are the hottest stars, with surface temperatures exceeding 30,000°C. Red stars are the coolest, with temperatures around 3,000°C.

questions.prompt: What is a star made of?
options: The Battle of the Somme (World War I)
questions.fact: Stars are made primarily of hydrogen and helium in a plasma state - a superheated gas where atoms are stripped of their electrons.

questions.prompt: How do stars produce energy?
questions.fact: Stars produce energy through nuclear fusion, where hydrogen atoms combine to form helium under extreme pressure and temperature, releasing enormous amounts of energy.

questions.prompt: What is the name of our galaxy?
questions.fact: The Milky Way is our home galaxy, a spiral galaxy containing billions of stars, including our Sun. It gets its name from its milky appearance in the night sky.

questions.prompt: What is a supernova?
questions.fact: A supernova is the explosive death of a massive star, one of the most energetic events in the universe, briefly outshining entire galaxies.

questions.prompt: How long does it take for light from the Sun to reach Earth?
questions.fact: Light from the Sun takes approximately 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel the 93 million miles to Earth, traveling at the speed of light.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Tennessee?

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Indiana?

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Wisconsin?

questions.prompt: How many hours are in a day?
questions.fact: There are 24 hours in a day, which is the time it takes for Earth to complete one rotation on its axis relative to the Sun.

questions.prompt: How many minutes are in an hour?
questions.fact: There are 60 minutes in an hour. This system of time measurement dates back to ancient Babylonian mathematics, which used a base-60 number system.

questions.prompt: How many seconds are in a minute?
questions.fact: There are 60 seconds in a minute, part of the sexagesimal (base-60) time system that has been used for thousands of years.

questions.prompt: How many days are in a week?
questions.fact: There are 7 days in a week, a system that dates back to ancient times and is based on the seven celestial bodies visible to the naked eye (Sun, Moon, and five planets).

questions.prompt: How many months are in a year?
questions.fact: There are 12 months in a year, based on the approximate number of lunar cycles (about 12.37) that occur in one solar year.

questions.prompt: How many days are in a year?
questions.fact: A common year has 365 days, while a leap year has 366 days. Leap years occur every 4 years to account for the extra 0.25 days in Earth's orbit around the Sun.

questions.prompt: What is a leap year?
options: A year that starts on Monday
questions.fact: A leap year has 366 days instead of 365, with an extra day (February 29) added to keep the calendar year synchronized with the astronomical year.

questions.prompt: How many time zones are there in the world?
questions.fact: There are 24 time zones in the world, one for each hour of the day, based on Earth's 24-hour rotation and divided roughly along lines of longitude.

questions.prompt: What is the name for the time when the Sun is directly overhead?
questions.fact: Noon (12:00 PM) is when the Sun is at its highest point in the sky, directly overhead at the local meridian. This is also called solar noon.

questions.prompt: What do AM and PM stand for?
questions.fact: AM stands for 'Ante Meridiem' (before midday) and PM stands for 'Post Meridiem' (after midday), used in the 12-hour clock system to distinguish morning from afternoon/evening.

questions.prompt: How many time zones are there in the world?
questions.fact: There are 24 time zones in the world, one for each hour of the day, based on Earth's 24-hour rotation and divided roughly along lines of longitude.

questions.prompt: Which country has the most time zones?
questions.fact: Russia spans 11 time zones, the most of any country in the world, due to its vast east-west extent across Eurasia.

questions.prompt: What is the time zone in New York called?
questions.fact: New York is in the Eastern Time Zone (ET), which is 5 hours behind Coordinated Universal Time (UTC-5) during standard time.

questions.prompt: What is the International Date Line?
options: An imaginary line where the date changes
questions.fact: The International Date Line is an imaginary line in the Pacific Ocean where the date changes. When you cross it going west, you gain a day; going east, you lose a day.

questions.prompt: What is UTC?
questions.fact: UTC stands for Coordinated Universal Time, the primary time standard by which the world regulates clocks and time. It's essentially the same as Greenwich Mean Time (GMT).

questions.prompt: What is daylight saving time?
questions.fact: Daylight saving time is the practice of moving clocks forward one hour in spring and back one hour in fall to make better use of daylight.

questions.prompt: Which country uses only one time zone despite its large size?
questions.fact: China uses only one time zone (China Standard Time) despite spanning what would naturally be 5 time zones, causing the sun to rise and set at unusual times in western China.

questions.prompt: What is the time difference between New York and London?
questions.fact: The time difference between New York and London varies: 5 hours during standard time (New York is behind) and 4 hours during daylight saving time.

questions.prompt: What is GMT?
questions.fact: GMT stands for Greenwich Mean Time, the mean solar time at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London. It's now largely replaced by UTC but is essentially the same.

questions.prompt: How many time zones does the United States have?
questions.fact: The United States has 6 time zones: Eastern, Central, Mountain, Pacific, Alaska, and Hawaii-Aleutian. However, the mainland U.S. has 4 main time zones.
